title: The far side of the bubble
description: Four rules for the bubble: own only what survives a ten-year blackout, sell on a schedule and pay the tax, never borrow, buy what it throws away.
body: Four companies will spend about $725 billion on data centers this year, up 77 percent on 2025, and for the first time most of that money isn't coming out of cash flow. AI-linked companies have issued roughly $140 billion of investment-grade bonds so far in 2026, about half of all investment-grade issuance in America. Alphabet sold a hundred-year bond in February to pay for chips it will depreciate in five or six. Meta's debt went from $36 billion to $84 billion in two and a half years. More than 80 percent of the S&P 500's gain this year has come from AI names, and if you strip them out the index is up about two percent.

I'm not saying this ends tomorrow. I'm saying it ends, because every capital cycle financed with other people's money has ended, and for someone my age the interesting question isn't how to call the top. It's how to come out the other side owning more of the world than you went in with. These are my four rules. They aren't sophisticated. In my experience the sophisticated people are the ones who get hurt.

The first rule is a ten-year test. Before I buy anything I ask whether the company would still be standing if the world shut down for ten years, or if something catastrophic hit the economy in year three. Not thriving, just standing. Coca-Cola (KO) passes. People drank the product through two world wars, a depression and a pandemic, and the company has paid a dividend every year since 1920. Restaurant Brands (QSR) passes: thirty thousand restaurants selling people the cheapest hot calories in their town, which is a demand that gets stronger in a crisis, not weaker. Meta (META) passes too, which surprises people. It owns the social graph of more than three billion humans, the graph doesn't depreciate, and whatever superintelligence turns out to be, the company has the cash flow to stay in that race from behind if it has to.

Now try the same test on SK Hynix, or Broadcom, or Marvell. They're fine companies. But ask ten people who own them what the company sells, to whom, and what happens to the price of that product when the buyer's capital budget gets cut in half. Most can't answer. They own a ticker that went up, and that's the only fact they know about it. The test isn't whether this is a good business. It's whether you understand what kills it, and whether it can be killed. High-bandwidth memory is a commodity with a cycle. A social graph isn't.

The second rule is don't get greedy, and know what greed feels like from the inside, because it doesn't feel like greed. What the people around you are experiencing is a number getting larger. That's a different thing from getting richer, and the number only stays theirs once they convert it, and almost nobody converts it. They call themselves long-term investors when the actual mechanism is fear of the capital gains tax, so they never sell, and then the market sells for them at a price they didn't choose. Pay the tax. Long-term federal capital gains top out at 23.8 percent. The bubble's discount has no cap. Decide in advance what you'll sell and when, write it down, and move the proceeds into a separate account you treat as sealed, so that future you can't talk present you out of the exit. If you want real structure there are legal forms of it: gifting appreciated shares, a charitable remainder trust, a donor-advised fund. What doesn't exist is a trick that makes a realized gain untaxed. Anyone selling you that trick is really selling you a reason never to sell, and never selling is how the paper wealth of 2000 and 2021 turned back into paper.

The third rule is no leverage. None. No margin, no options you don't fully understand, no loan against the portfolio to buy more portfolio. Cash in, shares out, that's it. Every bubble has some mechanism by which a correct long-term view gets liquidated at the bottom, and the mechanism is always a margin call. India's retail traders lost about $10 billion in derivatives last year. Korean margin debt is above 34 trillion won against an index that has more than doubled since the start of last year, and the forced selling there has already started. Some of those people might even be right about the thesis. Their balance sheet won't let them stay around to find out. The only money you can hold through a crash is money you can lose without getting a phone call.

The fourth rule is to buy what the bubble is making distressed, because a bubble is a sorting machine and right now it's sorting wrong. Capital is draining out of everything that isn't AI and into everything that is, and the exits are mispriced. Gold is about a quarter below its January record. Uber (UBER) sits near a 52-week low because the market decided robotaxis will eat it, while it throws off close to $10 billion of free cash a year. Netflix (NFLX) is down about 44 percent in twelve months over an advertising guidance cut. Brookfield (BN) owns ports, pipelines, transmission lines, the kind of assets that produce cash for fifty years no matter which model is state of the art. None of these are exciting. Unexciting, cash-positive businesses are where most wealth that outlives a cycle comes from.

Then hold cash on top. Real cash, boring cash, earning whatever it earns. When the correction comes, the companies that are real will still be real and the labs that matter will still matter. If Anthropic or OpenAI ever list, the time to buy is after the first drawdown, not on the first day. What won't survive is the layer that financed growth with debt it can't service when revenue misses: the data-center shells, the GPU lessors, the clouds with one customer. Over-financed companies die in every cycle, and not because the product was bad. Debt has a maturity date and hype doesn't.
The AI bubble will make a small number of people generationally wealthy. I'd bet almost none of them will be the ones who bought the most AI.

title: A cartel of one
description: Indonesia mines two of every three tonnes of nickel, tried to ration its own ore this year, and watched the rally round-trip in ten months.
body: On a stretch of coast in Central Sulawesi that was grassland in 2013 there's now a 2,000-hectare industrial park with about 85,000 workers, fifty-odd tenants, a two-gigawatt coal plant and $34.3 billion of mostly Chinese capital in the ground. The Morowali park is what a policy looks like when it works. In 2020 Indonesia banned the export of raw nickel ore. If you wanted the rock you had to build the furnace next to it, and the Chinese did. Indonesia mined just over 30 percent of the world's nickel that year. In 2025 it mined 2.6 million of the world's 3.9 million tonnes, two of every three.

Everyone else shrank to fit. Australian output fell 54 percent last year, and BHP (BHP) mothballed Nickel West in October 2024 and has promised only a review by February 2027. Philippine output fell 24 percent. Glencore (GLEN) guides to 70,000 to 80,000 tonnes this year, which is about ten days of Indonesia. The Indonesians did it with high-pressure acid leach plants built for under $1.5 billion apiece and ramped up inside a year. The Western plants of the last cycle, Goro and Ambatovy, cost nearly $6 billion each and took five years or more.

Now the price, which I assumed was high when I started writing this, and which turns out not to be. Nickel averaged $15,000 a tonne on the LME in 2025, down 11 percent on 2024. The monopolist flooded its own market. So in February Jakarta did what a cartel does and cut the 2026 ore quota to 260 to 270 million wet tonnes, about a third below what it had approved for 2025. The metal ran from $14,000 in December to $20,000 on May 6, the highest since 2024. Then Indonesia's imports of Philippine ore rose 66 percent, smelter utilisation fell from 84 to 76 percent, lines in Sulawesi dropped below half capacity, and by October the ministry was cutting its ore benchmark and getting supplementary quotas ready. The International Nickel Study Group flipped its 2026 call from a 32,000-tonne deficit to a 19,000-tonne surplus. Nickel closed at $15,605 on October 28, roughly where it was a year earlier, with 279,000 tonnes sitting in LME sheds. The whole rally round-tripped in ten months.

Indonesia owns the ore and China owns the furnaces, and when they disagree the furnace wins, because ore left in the ground costs nothing and a smelter left cold still owes the bank. In my own terms, the quota was set at compile time and renegotiated at runtime. Jakarta can't run OPEC on an industry whose members are its own largest investors, and the investors have noticed. Tsingshan is pitching a park in Madagascar, Lygend wants a stake in Tanzania's Kabanga, and foreign direct investment into Indonesia fell 6 percent in 2025. In late October the Chinese-owned plants were reportedly discussing halving their own intermediate output. So the producers are doing the rationing the state couldn't.

The cost of the boom lands where the quota doesn't reach. In June 2025 a Greenpeace video of stripped islands in Raja Ampat, an archipelago that holds about three quarters of the world's known coral species at the heart of the Coral Triangle, drew fifteen million views, and the president revoked four of the five permits there within days. The fifth belonged to Gag Nikel, a subsidiary of the state miner. Its suspension was lifted in September.

The Western answer, such as it is, is Talon Metals' (TLO) Tamarack deposit in Minnesota: 8.6 million indicated tonnes at 1.73 percent, Rio Tinto as partner, a Tesla offtake, $20.6 million from the Pentagon and a state scoping decision still pending. The company's own plan is production this decade, if the permits come. America imports 41 percent of the nickel it uses and nearly all of the primary metal, mostly from Canada and Norway, and none of that changes because a ministry in Jakarta changed a number.
A cartel of one turns out to be a country arguing with itself, and at the moment the furnaces are winning the argument.

title: A garden hose on the seabed
description: Six hundred cables carry nearly all intercontinental data, four companies own most of the new ones, and fewer than twenty ships exist to fix them.
body: On Saturday, September 6, 2025, two cables on the floor of the Red Sea off Jeddah stopped carrying light. One was SEA-ME-WE-4, the other IMEWE, both trunk lines between the Indian subcontinent and Europe, and a third, FALCON, went down with them. Within hours Microsoft was warning Azure customers about traffic routed through the Middle East, Cloudflare was measuring delays of up to 30 percent between India and Europe, and Pakistan and the Gulf were running slow. The International Cable Protection Committee's early read was a merchant ship dragging its anchor, and nobody has shown otherwise. Repairs were put at two to six weeks, because the ships need permits from several governments and have to cross a war zone to get there.

The physical object is smaller than most people picture. Across most of an ocean a submarine cable is about the width of a garden hose, and the fibres inside it are the width of a hair. There are 607 of them in service by TeleGeography's count this September, with another 102 planned, something over 1.5 million kilometres in all. The ICPC logs 150 to 200 faults a year, and 70 to 80 percent of them are fishing gear and anchors in shallow water. Sabotage is rare. It doesn't need to be common, though. The Red Sea carries about a quarter of the data between Asia and Europe through roughly fifteen cables threaded past one strait, and one anchor, if that's what it was, took out three of them on a Saturday.

The arithmetic from there gets uncomfortable. Satellites carry well under one percent of international traffic; the FCC's figure for the United States is 0.37 percent. Everything else, every cloud region and every set of model weights, is a wire on the seabed, and the wires increasingly belong to four companies. Google has stakes in more than 30 systems, Meta in about 20, and TeleGeography counts Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon as stakeholders in over two-thirds of the systems now planned. Before the 1990s cables were built by consortia of national carriers, AT&T, British Telecom, Telstra. Now the cloud lays its own. A National Bureau of Economic Research paper this year puts about 70 percent of global data across at least one American-owned cable, up from under 20 percent in the early nineties. People argue about whether the internet is centralised. On the seabed it always has been.

The laying is more concentrated still. Three firms build nearly everything: Alcatel Submarine Networks, 80 percent of which the French state bought from Nokia in 2024 for about €100 million; SubCom, the only American turnkey supplier, which Cerberus bought for $325 million in 2018 and which reached a record $4.7 billion backlog by 2024; and NEC. China's HMN Tech has most of the rest. Then there's the part nobody budgets for. Roughly 60 ships on earth can lay or mend a cable, and fewer than 20 of them do only repair. Eight of the sixty are under eighteen years old, nineteen are over thirty, the oldest dates from 1978, and the study TeleGeography wrote for the SubOptic Association last year has two-thirds of the maintenance fleet at the end of its working life by 2040. Replacing it would cost about $3 billion over fifteen years, which is what four cloud companies spend on data centres in a day and a half.

The owners of the cables are the people who least want you to think about them, because a cloud that's a wire is a cloud with a location. In May Iranian officials floated charging a fee on the cables under the Strait of Hormuz and putting their repair in Iranian hands, and an IRGC official has reportedly put the cables on the target list. Those lines carry less than one percent of global bandwidth. One repair ship sits inside the Gulf.
So nearly everything that crosses an ocean does it inside a garden hose, guarded by sixty ships and an assumption. I'd never thought about the ships before September, and now I can't stop.

title: Boiling off in Qatar
description: A third of the world's helium sits behind Hormuz. Spot has tripled, fabs are rationed, and nobody's model has a line for a Gulf peace.
body: In March about two hundred cryogenic containers of liquid helium were stranded at Ras Laffan in Qatar. Each held roughly a million dollars of gas four degrees above absolute zero, and each was losing its load to boil-off within five or six weeks whether or not a ship came. The ships didn't come. The Strait of Hormuz has been closed or contested since the United States and Israel struck Iran on February 28, and it carries about a fifth of the world's LNG and about a third of its helium.

The helium is the part nobody planned for. Qatar's North Field gas is 0.04 percent helium, nearly every atom of it an alpha particle shed by uranium or thorium in the rock below, and QatarEnergy strips it out as a by-product of liquefaction, a little over two billion cubic feet a year, sold to Air Liquide, Linde and Iwatani. Iranian drones shut Ras Laffan on March 2. Missiles on March 18 and 19 wrecked two LNG trains, which is 17 percent of Qatar's liquefaction and 14 percent of its helium, and the chief executive says rebuilding will take about three years. By August the helium plants were at a quarter of capacity. Force majeure on Qatari cargoes has just been extended to the end of December, the strait is moving maybe 60 percent of normal crude under a US blockade of Iranian ports, and at the end of October mediators were in Tehran.

So the price did what prices do when a third of supply disappears and there's no substitute. Spot helium had doubled by the third week of March, with Europe near $450 per thousand cubic feet. By October a former Air Liquide executive was putting the spot move at a tripling, and long-term contracts, which are about 98 percent of the market and slow to reprice, are reported up 40 to 60 percent. American exports are up 70 percent since the war began, most of it going to chipmakers in Korea, Taiwan and Singapore, because Exxon's LaBarge field in Wyoming is about a fifth of world supply and the United States, at 43 percent, is the only producer that can flex. Russia, the third producer, put helium under export permits in April. South Korea bought 65 percent of its helium from Qatar last year, and by June some Korean and Taiwanese fabs were getting half their normal volume. On October 23 the Department of Energy added helium to its critical materials list, and the first industry it named was semiconductors.

Why helium specifically, and not some other gas? It's the only substance still liquid at 4.2 kelvin. The niobium-titanium magnets in an MRI scanner or a fusion experiment only superconduct below about ten kelvin, so a 1.5-tesla scanner sits in 1,500 litres of the stuff and the periodic table offers nothing else. In a fab the atom's lightness is the point. Blown across the back of a wafer in the etch chamber, it carries heat to the chuck faster than any heavier gas, and it finds leaks in vacuum systems because nothing smaller exists to slip through them. Semiconductors take about a fifth of the world's helium, roughly half the tools in a fab touch it, and a wafer that doesn't get etched today is a GPU that doesn't ship next quarter.

What I think the market has wrong is this. It prices the war in Brent, which was above $117 in late October, and in Qatar's LNG, which is why European gas is above €95. It doesn't price the inputs that are too small to carry a futures contract and too essential to do without, and helium is one of several. I own Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, and all four of their capital plans assume the wafers get etched. A reopened strait is the cheapest upgrade to those plans on offer, and I haven't seen an analyst model with that line in it.

One more thing about helium, which I find a bit sad. Once it's released it never comes back, because it's too light for the planet to hold onto. Qatar's has been leaving, a container at a time, since March.

title: Qatar buys American
description: The world's second-largest LNG exporter just signed to buy 7 million tonnes a year of US gas. I think it's buying insurance on its own strait.
body: On October 22 QatarEnergy signed to buy 4 million tonnes a year of liquefied natural gas from Cheniere (LNG), half from Sabine Pass and half from Corpus Christi, at Henry Hub plus a fixed fee, through 2054. A week later it signed for 3 million more from Woodside's (WDS) plant in Louisiana, twenty years, first cargoes in 2030. The country that shipped 82 million tonnes of LNG in 2025, a fifth of everything traded on earth, is now, by its own energy minister's count, the largest buyer of American LNG, and he says the final number will be "much higher."

The reason is a date. On February 28 the United States and Israel began striking Iran, and Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, which carried a fifth of the world's LNG. In early March Iranian drones hit Ras Laffan, QatarEnergy halted production and declared force majeure. Then a missile strike disabled two of the fourteen trains there, 12.8 million tonnes a year, 17 percent of Qatar's capacity, with a repair time of three to five years. There was a ceasefire in April, an agreement in June, a collapse in July, and a US blockade of Iranian ports reimposed on July 14 that is still in force. The force majeure now runs to year-end. The Dutch benchmark passed €97 a megawatt-hour at the end of October, its highest since 2022, and Asian spot is above $31 per million British thermal units against $2.60 at Henry Hub.

If you read the Cheniere contract against that spread, it isn't really a gas purchase. Qatar has 77 million tonnes of capacity and is building toward 142. It doesn't need Louisiana molecules. What it has bought is an option on the strait: twenty years of gas that loads on a coast nobody can close, priced off the Gulf Coast and resold at whatever price the Gulf sets. The minister more or less said this out loud, that pipelines around Hormuz "can be also targets" and that these deals need no capital and earn money the day the strait shuts. The tenant of the most dangerous waterway on earth has gone and bought insurance in Texas.

This is where I part ways with the people pricing a golden decade for American gas. The supply wave was real before the war and it's still coming: 234 million tonnes a year of liquefaction is under construction or approved worldwide, nearly half of it American, on top of 525 already operating. Venture Global (VG) closed $8.6 billion for the second phase of CP2 in March. Commonwealth and Delfin followed. The Energy Department has approved more than 18.6 billion cubic feet a day of exports since the January 2025 order ended the permitting pause, and first-half exports ran 23 percent above last year. Most of that gas is sold at Henry Hub plus a fee, meaning the seller gets paid for liquefaction and the buyer owns the spread.

So the question I keep asking is what the spread looks like in 2030, when the plants being financed at today's $31 actually arrive. The IEA says the war delays the easing effect of the supply wave by at least two years and removes about 15 percent of the new supply expected through 2030. That's a delay, not a cancellation. Qatar's undamaged trains restart within a week of a peace deal, the first North Field expansion train is slated for early 2027, and the buyers shopping now did the opposite when the price spiked: Pakistan's first-half imports fell 47 percent, India burned coal, China took 12 percent less for four months. Demand at $31 is demand that has already started to leave. A liquefaction train is a thirty-year asset being sanctioned in an eight-month price spike, and a fixed fee only looks fixed until the person paying it runs the numbers on a $9 Asian market in 2031.

The strait will reopen at some point. Every contract signed this month is a bet on when, and the party with the best information about the answer is the one that has started buying. I notice that, and I'm not sure the gas bulls do.

title: Rationing a metal the chemists are deleting
description: Congo closed its border and cobalt went up fourfold. Now it's falling anyway, because the cathode chemistry that needed the metal is on its way out.
body: Every article about Congo's minerals has the number $24 trillion in it somewhere, and I have yet to find one that shows where it comes from, so I'm not going to use it. Here are some numbers somebody actually counted. In 2025 the Democratic Republic of Congo mined 230,000 of the world's 310,000 tonnes of cobalt, which is 73 percent, and it holds 6 million of the 12 million tonnes of known reserves. Half the metal still in the ground is in one country, and China refines about four fifths of what comes out of it.

On February 22, 2025, with cobalt under $10 a pound at a nine-year low, Kinshasa closed the border to it. Exports stopped for eight months. In October the ban turned into a quota: 96,600 tonnes a year for 2026 and 2027, 9,600 of them reserved for the state, from a country that had just mined 230,000. So exports were cut by more than half by decree, without a mine closing or an ore body running out. I can't think of a purer price-setting experiment any commodity has run this decade.

For about a year it worked. Cobalt averaged $21 a pound in the US in 2025 against $16.77 in 2024. Hydroxide out of Congo roughly quadrupled from where it sat before the ban, and by late April 2026 metal was being assessed near $56,000 a tonne. Then the quota ran into the one variable it doesn't control. By August the agency that sets it was saying it might cut the quota further "to help restore market balance," which is the phrase a cartel uses when the price is falling. On October 28 cobalt was about $34,600 a tonne, down 29 percent in a year and 12 percent in a month.

You can tell what the miners think from how they responded. CMOC (3993.HK), which is Chinese, runs Tenke Fungurume and Kisanfu and produced 117,549 tonnes last year, more than half of Congo's output and about 38 percent of the world's, out of two mines. It kept its 2026 guidance at 100,000 to 120,000 tonnes against an estimated export quota of around 31,000, so most of what it digs is going into a stockpile to wait. Glencore (GLEN) went the other way. Its cobalt output fell 46 percent in the first half of 2026, Mutanda produced none, and the company now says its Congolese assets prioritise copper, with the cobalt held in solution to be sold "as export regulations evolve." Copper is at a record, so that's an easy call. Cobalt is the thing you leave in the tank. For scale, Canada, where cobalt comes up as a byproduct of nickel, mined 3,500 tonnes in 2025, which is about eleven days of CMOC. Indonesia mined 44,000, 14 percent of the world, as a byproduct of its nickel acid-leach plants, and no quota written in Kinshasa reaches it.

The bigger problem for Congo is that it's rationing a metal the battery industry has spent a decade designing out. Cobalt's job in a cathode is structural. It keeps the layered nickel-manganese oxide lattice ordered while lithium moves in and out, and stops nickel wandering into lithium's sites. Lithium iron phosphate uses a phosphate framework that's rigid enough to need no cobalt at all, and LFP took 51 percent of the global battery market in 2024 and 79 percent of that year's growth. Cobalt-bearing chemistries fell from 60 to 53 percent of EV battery demand in a single year. Even inside the chemistries that still use it, going from an equal nickel-manganese-cobalt mix to the 8:1:1 formula cuts the cobalt per kilowatt-hour by more than half. An EV carries five to ten kilograms. The number is falling by share and by dose at the same time.

OPEC rations a molecule nobody has replaced. Kinshasa is rationing one that already has a replacement with a lower bill of materials and a better safety record, and every month the price sits above the cost of switching, a few more cathode lines switch. I don't think the quota creates any demand. If anything it brings forward the day the demand leaves. It runs to the end of 2027, and I doubt the chemistry waits that long.

title: Seventeen years for 400 points, eighteen months for 7,000
description: Seventeen years took the KOSPI from 2,000 to 2,400. Eighteen months took it to 9,385. Margin debt did the last leg, and margin runs both ways.
body: On October 15, Korean brokerages sold 80.5 billion won of their customers' shares without asking them. A week earlier the daily figure had been 6.4 billion. In between, the KOSPI fell seven sessions in a row, from about 6,900 to 5,500, and the margin loans underneath it, which had gone back above 34 trillion won on October 13 for the first time since July, started shrinking the only way they shrink quickly, which is by being called.

The run-up needs dates to make sense. The KOSPI first closed above 2,000 in July 2007. It ended 2024 at 2,399, with one year above 3,000 in 2021. So seventeen years, four hundred points, and a whole literature on the Korea discount.

Then it closed above 4,000 last October, 5,000 in January, 6,000 in February, 7,000 in May, 8,000 three weeks after that, 9,000 in June, and touched 9,385 on June 19. Seven thousand points in eighteen months. It then fell 44 percent in six weeks, to 5,263 on July 29, recovered to 7,100 by September, and gave up a fifth again in the first half of October. It closed at 6,012 on October 28 and 5,938 on October 29. I don't think that's the chart of a stock market. It's the chart of a margin account.

The awkward thing is that the earnings are real. SK Hynix reported at the end of October: revenue of 104.6 trillion won, up 328 percent, an operating margin of 79.7 percent, memory sold out through 2029. Samsung made 107 trillion won of operating profit in the same quarter and promised 90 to 110 trillion won of dividends and buybacks. So you've got two companies sitting on top of an index in a country where more than half of last quarter's growth surprise came from chips, private consumption fell at its fastest rate in four and a half years, and bank delinquencies are at a ten-year high. The index is basically the memory cycle, and the country is a lot more than that.

The retail response to all this was to borrow. Margin loans went from 28.9 trillion won at the end of July to 34.3 trillion by October 12, up nearly a fifth, while cash sitting in brokerage accounts fell 7 percent to 96.9 trillion. A market without leverage damps its own swings, because a lower price finds a buyer. A market carrying 34 trillion won of margin amplifies them, because a lower price finds a margin clerk.

Forced sales rose 12.7-fold in a week, unsettled receivables reached 1.24 trillion won, and the margin balance dropped almost a trillion in a single day. It has since settled below 30 trillion, and on October 27 retail investors net sold 949 billion won while foreigners bought. The forced selling did what the dip couldn't and broke the loop, at least for now.

The government hasn't exactly been a bystander either. On October 29 the president's senior secretary for policy apologised in the National Assembly for single-stock leveraged ETFs, products that pay twice a stock's daily move, whose launch, as he put it, coincided with a period of repricing. Daily double leverage in a market that moves 6 percent on a Wednesday turns volatility into losses even when the stock ends up where it began, and the state waved those products through.

So I think this is a reset, and I won't pretend to know the date. What I can say is what has already happened: the index has been cut 44 percent once and 20 percent once inside four months, and the forced selling that did the second cut started with margin debt at 34 trillion won. The next leg begins wherever the margin balance sits when memory prices stop rising, and memory prices have never not stopped rising. Hynix says the shortage runs through 2030. The whole trade is a bet on that word, through.

The photograph above these stories is usually the same one, a wall of screens in the dealing room at Hana Bank's head office in Jung-gu, showing the KOSPI and the KOSDAQ. The screens show the index. I've never seen one that showed the loans.

title: Sixteen years on a five-year chip
description: Digital Realty just had its best quarter ever and I still pass: six tenants, sixteen-year leases on five-year hardware, and power it doesn't own.
body: After the close on October 29, Digital Realty (DLR) reported what I think is the best quarter a data-centre landlord has ever reported. Revenue of $1.9 billion, up 21 percent. New leases worth $855 million a year of rent, a record. A backlog of signed leases not yet paying of $2.5 billion, also a record. Guidance raised, dividend covered, a Moody's upgrade in hand. The stock rose less than two percent after hours, to about $186, which is 22 times this year's core funds from operations for a company whose tenants can't sign fast enough.

I read the same release a second time pretending I was a lender, and it looked different. Of the $627 million of new rent at Digital Realty's own share, $474 million, three quarters of it, came from hyperscale deals above a megawatt, and the three largest were 60 megawatts or more each. Management offers it as diversification that six different hyperscalers have been the top signer over the last seven quarters. Another way to say that is six customers drive the business. The weighted average lease it signed runs about sixteen years. It takes seventeen months from signature to the first rent cheque. The development pipeline, about 1.5 gigawatts under construction, is 63 percent pre-leased, so the other 37 percent is being built on faith, and the company will spend $4.25 to $4.75 billion on it this year, against $2.9 billion of shares sold into the market since January and about $19.5 billion of debt outstanding.

Nobody puts the mismatch on a slide, so here it is. The landlord signs for sixteen years. The tenant depreciates the hardware inside the building over five or six, and the only reason anyone wants a 60-megawatt hall in Indianapolis is that a capital budget in Seattle or Mountain View says so this year. Jefferies counted more than 80 percent of the S&P 500's gain this year, through May, as coming from AI names, and without them the index was up about two percent. The tenants' appetite for halls comes from that same enthusiasm. So you have a REIT being paid rent by the boom, which has promised its own lenders the rent will keep arriving long after the chips in the racks are scrap.

The Rust compiler refuses a reference that outlives the value it points at. A sixteen-year lease on a hall whose tenant's reason to be there gets written off in five is pretty much that reference. Real estate doesn't have a borrow checker. It has a credit cycle, and the check runs at the worst possible moment.

Then there's power, which the landlord doesn't own either. Digital Realty's own call mentioned the long queues and constraints across Ohio and the nine-cent power in Indiana it moved toward instead. A data centre is a transformer with an office attached. The asset the tenant actually needs is the utility interconnection, which the REIT rents from a monopoly on terms it doesn't set. An analyst on the call put the build cost at roughly $15 million a megawatt. That's the price of a building whose value depends on a wire the builder doesn't control and a tenant whose budget it never sees.

I'm not short, to be clear. Shorting a landlord with a $2.5 billion backlog and investment-grade tenants is how people lose money arguing with a cycle. I own the tenants instead: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta. If the capex holds, they get the compute and I get the earnings. If it doesn't, they stop signing, and the stopping shows up first in the backlog of whoever built the shell. Equinix (EQIX) runs the other model, thousands of tenants renting cabinets and cross-connects rather than six renting halls, and if I were going to look at a data-centre REIT at all that's the one I'd start with. The newer single-tenant landlords are Digital Realty's trade with even fewer customers.

Maybe the leases all get honoured and I've talked myself out of a good stock. That has happened before. But I keep coming back to the fact that the landlord has lent a building for sixteen years to a reason that lasts five, and nobody on the call seemed to think that was worth a question.

title: The $2.8 billion consolation prize
description: Netflix won the streaming war, got paid $2.8 billion to lose the bidding war, and sits at a 52-week low. I own a lot and I'd like an activist.
body: In February Paramount wired Netflix (NFLX) $2.8 billion for the privilege of buying Warner Bros. Discovery instead of it. Netflix had agreed in December to take the studio and HBO for $82.7 billion, then went all-cash at $27.75 a share in January. Paramount came over the top at $31, about $111 billion for all of Warner rather than just the studios, and Warner's board took it. Netflix declined to raise. The deal closed on October 6 and the combined company is called Skydance. So Netflix walked away with the break fee, no $83 billion acquisition to digest, and a share price that has since fallen through the floor.

I should say up front that I own a large position, so read the rest accordingly. The stock closed at $62.05 on October 29, a 52-week low, down about 44 percent in a year from a high of $116.73. The quarter that did the damage, reported October 20, was a beat by any normal reading: revenue of $12.9 billion up 12 percent, operating margin of 34.6 percent against 28.2 a year ago, earnings up 47 percent, $4.8 billion of buybacks, the most it has ever done. It got punished for cutting its 2026 advertising forecast from about $3 billion to about $2.7 billion, and for a line in the letter admitting to "some investor concern about our view hours growth."

So, three hundred million dollars of ads arriving a few quarters late, from a company that will do $51 billion of revenue this year at a 31.5 percent margin and generate $12 billion of free cash. The market took about $200 billion off the valuation for that. I've read the letter three times and I still can't make those two numbers fit together.

The war is over and Netflix won it. The world holds 2.24 billion online video subscriptions and spent $176 billion on them last year, passing pay television for the first time. Netflix had more than 325 million of those paying households at the end of last year, by far the most, and it's the only pure streamer earning a margin a packaged-goods company would envy. What's left of the competition is a division of a phone maker, a retailer and a theme-park operator, plus Skydance, which lined up $54 billion of debt commitments to assemble a library. The American household holds about four paid video services and pays about $69 a month for them, and 73 percent say they're tired of the price rises. Churn across the industry runs near 40 percent a year. Netflix's churn after this year's increases came in better than it forecast.

Which gets me to what I actually want, and the irony in wanting it. Pershing Square bought about 3.1 million Netflix shares in January 2022 and sold them in April after a subscriber miss, booking a loss above $400 million. Its founder wrote at the time that he had lost confidence in his ability to predict the company. The shares then went up roughly fivefold before the split. I would like Pershing Square, or anyone with its temperament and a bit more patience, back on the register, because the argument isn't complicated. Netflix spends about 1.1 times its amortisation on content and doesn't need to spend more. It needs to say so, cap the budget, and return the rest. This year it raised prices in the United States, Mexico and Spain and the members stayed. There's $22.3 billion of buyback authority sitting there and a share price it can retire at about 20 times this year's earnings. The content arms race ended on October 6, and I'd like someone to tell the capital budget.

Uber (UBER), which I also own, is the same trade in a different industry. Both went from growth at any price to disciplined cash machines with an advertising layer bolted on, both generate $10 to $12 billion of free cash a year, and both sit at 52-week lows because the market, having spent a decade demanding they grow up, has apparently decided grown-up companies are boring.
Netflix was paid $2.8 billion to lose. The market has charged it $200 billion for winning, and I've been buying more.

title: A truck with no driver still needs a dispatcher
description: Driverless trucks are late, real and about to get cheap. I think the money ends up with whoever has the loads, so I own Uber, not Aurora.
body: Aurora (AUR) put out its third-quarter letter on October 28 and the number that jumped out at me was twenty. That's how many driverless trucks it has built. In February the target was two hundred by the end of the year, and that has quietly become the end of next February. Revenue guidance went from a $15 million midpoint to $9 million, the quarter brought in $3 million against a $234 million net loss, and a company valued at close to $10 billion dropped 7 percent after hours. Kodiak (KDK), down 87 percent since it listed last year, signed its first binding highway contract around the same time: seventy-five trucks for a carrier in Fresno, starting in 2028. Tesla's Semi finally reached volume production in September, seven years late, and it isn't autonomous.

I don't want to be unfair to Aurora. Its trucks have run half a million commercial miles with nobody on board, including the thousand-mile run from Fort Worth to Phoenix that no human is legally allowed to drive without stopping. It's promising a thousand trucks by the end of 2027, and one carrier has signed up for five hundred of them, non-binding. The $250 million it expects to burn this quarter is the binding part.

A figure I kept hearing this year, 1,300 percent growth to 2036, turns out not to be Goldman's at all. It's a research shop's forecast of a $1.3 billion market last year becoming $17.7 billion. Goldman's actual April note is more useful to me: a $560 billion global market by 2035, cost parity with a human driver in the US around 2028, and a cost per mile falling from $8.56 today to $2.03, against a driver at $2.55 now and $2.84 then. If a truck runs 80 cents a mile cheaper than a person and never hits an hours-of-service limit, it doesn't have to be clever. It just has to be legal.

What the forecast skips, I think, is what the business looks like once the driver is software. The truck becomes a commodity that Volvo and Paccar build on their existing lines, and the driver becomes a per-mile licence sold by two or three vendors who can't really hold a price against each other. Aurora and Kodiak both describe themselves as asset-light, meaning the carrier buys the truck and rents the driver by the mile. Fine, but then where does the money go? To whoever has the loads. Matching freight to trucks across a continent is a demand problem, and there's one company that has spent sixteen years on nothing else.

I own Uber (UBER). The market has decided it's a ride-hailing company about to be eaten by robotaxis. It closed at $65.78 on October 27, a 52-week low, 35 percent below its high, at fourteen times trailing earnings, having just produced $10 billion of trailing free cash flow for the first time. Bookings grew 24 percent last quarter. Waymo did leave Uber's app in Phoenix in July and plans its own in Austin and Atlanta in 2028, but it runs about 4,000 cars. Uber did 3.9 billion trips in a quarter, and under half a percent of them were autonomous. So the disruption is real and it's small, and the stock is priced as if it were large and certain.

The freight side is the part nobody seems to model. Uber Freight manages more than $20 billion of freight. Aurora, Volvo's autonomous unit and Waabi have all hauled its loads between Dallas and Houston. Uber owns a piece of Aurora from selling it its own self-driving unit back in 2020, and it backed Waabi's funding round. It builds no truck and writes no driver. The way I'd put it in Rust is that Uber is a trait: the caller never learns which concrete type is behind it, only that the method is implemented. The market is pricing the trait as if it were one of the implementations.

The counter-argument is a serious one and I go back and forth on it. A demand layer only has power while supply is fragmented. If Waymo ends up with most of the robotaxis and two companies end up with most of the trucks, they'll sell direct and Uber's take rate becomes a toll the owners won't pay. The founder of Uber Freight left last year to run operations at Waabi, which tells you something about where he thinks the power sits.

My bet is still the other way, mostly because every autonomy company I look at is turning into a thin-margin seller of software by the mile, and none of them has a customer. A truck with no driver still needs somebody to tell it where to go, and I'd rather own that somebody than the truck.

title: Every wire on earth, again
description: The money for the grid is finally showing up. The transformers aren't. Electrification is limited by a queue now, not a budget.
body: Every power line on earth, strung end to end, comes to about 80 million kilometres. The IEA's count of what has to be added or replaced by 2040 to meet the targets governments have already signed is also 80 million kilometres. Not a share of it. The whole grid, again, in fourteen years, while the first one stays switched on.

The grid is the oldest machine most countries still run at full load. It has delivered power for over a century, and for most of this one it was treated as finished. Global grid investment sat flat at roughly $300 billion a year while everyone argued about generation. The IEA's grids report said the figure had to pass $600 billion by 2030, and its 2026 investment report has network spending at about $550 billion this year, up nearly a fifth in twelve months. So the money, for once, is arriving.

What isn't arriving is the equipment. A large power transformer now takes up to four years to secure. High-voltage cable takes two to three years, direct-current cable more than five, and transformer prices are up about 75 percent since 2019 while cable prices have roughly doubled. Building a new high-voltage line takes seven years or more, against one to three for a data centre. More than 2,500 gigawatts of generation, storage and large loads are stuck in connection queues worldwide, about 150 gigawatts of them data centres. In the whole of the last decade the world built about 1.5 million kilometres of new transmission.

I think the physics of this is the whole story, so bear with me. Any driven system has a relaxation time, and if you force it faster than it can relax it never settles into a new equilibrium. It just lags the drive. A grid relaxes over five to fifteen years. The thing driving it, a hyperscaler's capital budget, changes every quarter. On a utility's books that lag goes by the name of the interconnection queue.

Then there's the demand the wire is supposed to carry, which I had wrong in my own notes. The world used about 28,200 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, three percent more than the year before, and the IEA expects 33,600 by 2030, so roughly 1,100 terawatt-hours a year of new demand against 700 a year over the previous decade. The United States uses about 4,200. In other words the world is adding a United States of demand every four years, and in the IEA's central scenario it adds more than two of them by 2035. Most people assume that's AI, and globally it mostly isn't. Data centres are less than a tenth of the growth, and the peak is set by air conditioning. America is the exception: data centres are about half of the 420-plus terawatt-hours it's on course to add by 2030.

That's where American Electric Power (AEP) comes in. Its summer peak was about 37 gigawatts last year. By May it had signed agreements for 63 gigawatts of new load by 2030, 41 of them in Texas, most of it data centres. They came to AEP because it owns about 2,100 miles of 765-kilovolt line, nine tenths of what exists in the country. Its five-year capital plan rose a third to $72 billion last October, then to $78 billion in May, then to $100 billion on October 28, with the rate base compounding at 13 percent or better through 2031. The release talks about "up to $21 billion of fixed cost offsets for residential customers," which in plain language means that under the old tariffs you paid for the hyperscaler's substation and under the new ones in Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky and West Virginia the hyperscaler does. Last October AEP guided residential rates up 3.5 percent a year, and it earns a regulated return on every dollar either way. If I owned a utility it would be the one that owns the wire everyone else is waiting for.
The power itself crosses the state in milliseconds. The wire it needs shows up in 2033, if the transformer order holds.

title: The bleach that stayed in the bottle
description: Clorox peaked at $240 in 2020 and is $87 now. The safe-haven trade works for about one quarter in twenty, and you pay for it in the other nineteen.
body: Clorox (CLX) closed at $239.87 on August 5, 2020. That was the week it reported the fastest sales growth in its history, with every canister of disinfecting wipes in America sold before it reached a shelf. On October 28 this year it closed at $87.36, after touching $79.12 on October 1. It's 64 percent below a record that is six years old, and the whole company is worth about $10.5 billion. Nothing about the product changed. Bleach is sodium hypochlorite in water and it does the same thing to a kitchen counter now that it did in 2019. What changed was how scared people were, and in 2020 fear was the only thing the price was measuring.

The pitch I still hear for this stock is that household products are where you hide. Usually someone cites a bank study showing home-goods companies beat the S&P 500 in volatile periods. I went looking for that study and couldn't find it, but I don't think it's needed, because the public record says the same thing. In 2022 the S&P 500 returned minus 18.5 percent and consumer staples lost less than one percent. In February this year, with tech selling off, staples led the index by 13 points. Clorox has a beta of 0.57. When the market falls, this stock falls less. I'm not disputing any of that.

What the pitch leaves out is what the hiding place costs in the years without a crash, which is most of them. The staples trade is basically a put option with an expensive premium. Over the twelve months to October 2025 the sector returned minus 0.7 percent against 15.5 for the index. Clorox is down 27 percent in a year when the market went up. Its 52-week high of $128.90 came in February, during the volatility, and by October the volatility had passed and so had the bid.

The company has also had a rough few years at the one thing it's supposed to be good at, which is being boring. In August 2023 a cyberattack took down its order systems, slowed its factories and knocked about $356 million off a quarter's sales, roughly a fifth. In 2025 it moved its US business onto a new ERP system, the kind of migration that's supposed to be invisible. Retailers stocked up ahead of the switch and then ran inventories down, and Clorox says that cost fiscal 2026 7.5 points of sales and 90 cents of earnings. Net sales fell 5 percent to $6.72 billion and earnings fell 26 percent to $4.81 a share. Then in April it closed the $2.25 billion purchase of GOJO, the maker of Purell, mostly with debt, which takes borrowings to about $5 billion. A company that peaked on pandemic hygiene has just paid two billion dollars for more pandemic hygiene.

The dividend is the one thing that has behaved. Clorox has raised it for 48 consecutive years by the count I found (I've only seen that figure in one place, so take it as roughly right), most recently by a cent to $1.25 a quarter. At $87 the yield is 5.7 percent and the payout is 103 percent of trailing earnings. That ratio comes down if the ERP comparison washes out and GOJO adds the 9.5 points of sales promised for fiscal 2027. It doesn't come down if the CEO's own word for the operating environment, "challenging," turns out to be the accurate one.

So what is this stock? My best description is a phase-change artifact. In 2020 fear pushed the market across a boundary where the only thing anyone wanted to hold was the thing that kills germs, and Clorox got priced as if that state were permanent. It wasn't, as it turned out. The system relaxed, the premium evaporated, and what's left is a slow-growing bleach company at 18 times trailing earnings with debt it didn't have before.

I don't own it. I wouldn't short it either, because a 5.7 percent yield and a 0.57 beta will beat the index in the next crash, and there will be one. But the safe trade is only safe for the quarter when nobody wants anything else. The other nineteen quarters it's a stock like any other, with worse growth, and you pay for the insurance in every one of them.

title: Three hundred thousand dollars a bed
description: Two companies hold most of ICE detention. Washington now buys their buildings, pays them to keep running them, and can't FOIA either one.
body: On July 2 the Department of Homeland Security paid CoreCivic (CXW) $1.5 billion for two detention centers in California, and on August 4 another $734 million for two more in Kansas and Minnesota. That's 7,187 beds for $2.2 billion, which the company's own release works out to $307,000 a bed. On October 5 GEO Group (GEO) sold its Adelanto complex in the Mojave, 2,644 beds, for $950 million, or $359,000 a bed. ICE's median daily rate for a bed is $92. In every one of these deals the seller stays on to run the building. GEO's contract runs to 2029 with an option to 2034. So the government bought the asset and kept the operator.

The line you hear, that two companies own half of America's private prisons, is roughly true and misses the point. Private prisons hold about 8 percent of state and federal prisoners, and GEO and CoreCivic are most of that trade, but prisons aren't where the money is anymore. Immigration detention is. About a third of ICE detainees sit in GEO facilities and roughly a quarter of ICE's beds are CoreCivic's, and 86 percent of detainees were in for-profit hands when this administration took office. ICE was 48 percent of GEO's $2.63 billion of revenue last year and about 42 percent of CoreCivic's in the first quarter of this one. Between them the two booked about $4.8 billion in 2025.

What changed is one number. On January 20, 2025 ICE held 39,314 people. By July 30 this year the average daily population was 67,180, after a January peak above 73,000, and the count of authorized facilities had doubled from 134 to 272. The law signed on July 4, 2025 put $45 billion into detention through September 2029, against an annual detention appropriation that had been running at about $3.8 billion. GEO took its ICE capacity from about 20,000 beds to 26,000 in a year, the most new business in its history. CoreCivic now guides to $1.5 billion of net income in 2026, because selling four buildings to your largest customer books as a $1.8 billion gain. Both companies raised their buybacks within days of closing, GEO to $1.25 billion, CoreCivic to $1.2 billion with $500 million of it executed immediately.

The other complaint I hear is that these companies owe the government nothing, and I think that has it backwards. They're contractors, and in this contract the obligations mostly run toward them. ICE agreements carry guaranteed minimums, beds paid for nightly whether anyone sleeps in them, and an analysis of ICE's own July data found about 8,200 such beds standing empty at more than $1.2 million a day. The GAO's September report is titled, in full, Immigration Detention: Urgent Planning Needed to Avoid Further Waste of Taxpayer Dollars. What flows the other way is harder to see. The Freedom of Information Act doesn't reach a private operator, and a bill to change that has been introduced since 2005 and never passed. ICE's detention standards aren't written into law. The acting director of ICE since June spent about a decade as a GEO executive. Thirty-nine people died in ICE custody in the twelve months to January, the most in any year since the agency was created in 2003, and twenty-seven of them died in privately run facilities.

I wouldn't own either stock, and my reason is structural before it's moral. Every business I own has a growth metric I can reason about: subscribers, payment volume, syrup. The growth metric here is the number of human beings the executive branch decides to confine, which went from 39,000 to 73,000 in a year and which the next administration, appropriations fight or court order can move the other way with a signature. GEO has traded between $12.51 and $33.17 over the past twelve months and closed at $27.57 on October 28, at thirteen times earnings. To me that looks less like the chart of a business than the chart of a referendum.
The government owns the buildings now. The companies are still paid by the bed, and I don't see what's supposed to change that.

title: Six times the demand, the same price
description: Lithium demand has grown six-fold since 2017 and the price is back where it started. The rock was never the scarce part.
body: In the middle of May a tonne of battery-grade lithium carbonate traded above 200,000 yuan on the Guangzhou futures exchange, a two-year high. On October 22 the main contract closed at 94,180. In dollars, Fastmarkets' seaborne assessment went from $24.50 to $25.80 a kilogram on May 11 to $12.80 to $15.00 on October 27. Nothing happened to the metal in between. Zimbabwe halted concentrate exports in February, a CATL mine in Jiangxi stayed shut, and the market decided there was a shortage. Then two Australian mines restarted, China's main price reporter restated national inventory upward by roughly 100,000 tonnes in a single September morning, and a bearish Goldman note on October 12 helped take the contract down 11.8 percent in a day.

If I were going to own lithium at all I'd own the people who dig it rather than the futures, and the last five months are a decent illustration of why neither has been comfortable. The chemistry is what keeps pulling me back to this, so let me at least get it right. Lithium is element three, the lightest metal there is, and its standard reduction potential is about minus 3.04 volts, the most negative on the table, which is why it sits at the anode. A cell built on lithium delivers more voltage than one built on anything else. Energy is charge times voltage, and lithium supplies both terms, the most volts per cell and, because each atom weighs almost nothing, the most charge per gram. That's the entire bull case, and it's true.

What the bull case leaves out is the supply response. In 2017 the world consumed about 41,500 tonnes of lithium and battery-grade carbonate averaged $13,900 a tonne. In 2025 the world consumed about 263,000 tonnes, more than six times as much, and the American annual average price was $9,000. Batteries went from 46 percent of demand to 88. So demand did exactly what the decks promised, and the price, after a visit to $63,700 in 2022, came all the way back down, because lithium isn't scarce. It's dissolved in salt flats and locked in hard rock across Australia, Zimbabwe, Brazil, Mali and Argentina, and every one of those places answered the 2022 price within three years. Scarcity turned out to be a story about rocks, and price a story about how fast people can dig, and people were quick.

The geography is the part I find beautiful, for what it's worth. Under the salt crust of the Salar de Atacama in northern Chile the brine gets pumped up into ponds, and the desert sun does the first stage of refining for free. That salar, Chile's corner of the lithium triangle it shares with Argentina and Bolivia, gave the world 56,000 tonnes last year. That's a fifth of mine supply, not the 30 percent people still quote (I quoted it myself until I checked the USGS table). Australia's hard rock gave 92,000 and China 62,000. SQM (SQM), which pumps the Atacama alongside Albemarle (ALB), folded its operation last December into a joint venture with the state copper company that runs to 2060, which is Chile's way of saying it has noticed what the brine is worth.

The majors have voted with cash. Rio Tinto (RIO) paid $6.7 billion for Arcadium in March 2025, buying Argentine brine near the bottom of the cycle. Standard Lithium (SLI) and Equinor are a final investment decision away from pulling 22,500 tonnes a year of carbonate out of the Smackover brine under southwest Arkansas, with $225 million from the Department of Energy attached and first production pencilled in for 2028. Until then the United States has one producing operation, Albemarle's ponds at Silver Peak, Nevada, so small that the Geological Survey withholds its output to protect the company. A country paying for a battery supply chain mines almost none of the lithium that goes in it.

One last thing I like about this element. Lithium carbonate was a psychiatric drug long before it was a battery. An Australian doctor started giving it to manic patients in 1949, and medicine is still about one percent of demand. It has been steadying minds for seventy-seven years. It has never once steadied a price.

title: Four people and a gallon of diesel
description: The first coast-to-coast railroad in American history will be approved or killed by four board members, on a clock that runs out in August 2027.
body: A gallon of diesel moves a ton of freight nearly 500 miles on an American railroad. Union Pacific (UNP) burned 1.034 gallons per thousand gross ton-miles last quarter, and that number falls a percent or two every year because the physics is on its side. A steel wheel on a steel rail deforms by microns, a rubber tyre on asphalt by centimetres, and rolling resistance is the energy you lose putting the deformation back. Rail moves about 40 percent of long-distance ton-miles for 1.8 percent of transport emissions. Nothing on land comes close, and no single company has ever run the whole distance.

Union Pacific would like to be the first. On July 29, 2025 it agreed to buy Norfolk Southern for one share plus $88.82 in cash, $320 a share at the time and about $85 billion of enterprise value, promising $2.75 billion a year in savings and more than 50,000 route miles across 43 states, Pacific to Atlantic, under one dispatcher. Shareholders of both companies approved it in November with more than 99 percent of the votes. If the regulator says no, Union Pacific pays Norfolk Southern $2.5 billion and walks away.

The regulator is the Surface Transportation Board, and the next decade of American freight is being settled inside a calendar almost nobody reads. In January the Board rejected the first application as incomplete, because the railroads had projected no market shares past closing and had left out the part of the merger agreement that defines when Union Pacific may walk. A revised filing arrived April 30, the Board accepted it on May 28 and then froze the case to get more detail on captive shippers, diversion and gateways. It lifted the freeze on August 18 and set the clock: comments November 18, replies February 16, briefs May 28, a decision by August 28, 2027. In September it refused to throw the case out early, as BNSF, CSX and five shipper groups had asked, saying only that a deal of first impression deserved a full record.

First impression is the phrase to watch. This is the first merger to be judged under rules the Board wrote in 2001 and has never once used, which require a Class I combination to enhance competition rather than just preserve it. The opponents say a coast-to-coast carrier can't pass that test because its whole point is to remove the interchange, and the interchange is where a shipper gets a second quote. Union Pacific's answer is that the real competitor is the truck, and that autonomous trucks with no driver to pay or rest will take share from a network that loses a day or two at every hand-off. Its chief executive told a television interviewer in September he was 99.99 percent sure of approval and needs no divestitures. The chemical, fertilizer and grain shippers who would be left with one railroad in a lot of places are less sure, and they're the ones who pay the rate.

My own view is that the shippers are right about the mechanism and the railroads are right about the truck, and the Board has to pick which of two true things it fears more. What bothers me is who gets to pick. Five seats, four members: a chairman named by the President in January 2025, a vice chairman, a Democrat whose term runs to 2030, and a rail consultant sworn in this June. The fifth seat has been empty since the previous chairman was removed in August 2025 with no cause stated, a removal that the Supreme Court's June ruling on independent agencies made all but unreviewable. Nobody has been nominated to fill it. There's no veto above these four, no appeal except to a court that defers to them, and no ballot with their names on it.

The decision will arrive as a press release with a number on it like 26-23. The railroad it describes will last a hundred years. I couldn't have named the four people deciding it before I started reading the docket, and I'd guess you couldn't either.

title: The chokehold is in the chemistry
description: China mines 60 percent of magnet rare earths and separates 91 percent. The leverage was never in the ground. It's in the solvent.
body: A kilogram of dysprosium oxide costs about $200 in China this month and somewhere between $2,500 and $5,500 outside it. Terbium oxide is $900 inside and $10,000 to $13,000 out. Same molecule, same purity, a factor of ten to twenty for crossing a border. That spread is the price of a Chinese export licence, and the licence regime producing it has now been in force for eighteen months, through three summits and two suspensions, with no sign of being lifted.

The dates matter, because people keep running them together. On April 4, 2025, Beijing put seven heavy rare earths, dysprosium and terbium among them, under case-by-case licensing. On October 9 it went much further: five more elements, controls on separation equipment, and an extraterritorial rule that would have required a Chinese licence for any magnet made anywhere containing 0.1 percent by value of Chinese material. When Trump and Xi met in Busan on October 30, China suspended the October package for a year, and Washington suspended its own Entity List affiliates rule, cut the fentanyl tariff and paused port fees. The April controls were never part of that deal. They're still there. Yttrium exports to the United States fell from over 333 tonnes in the eight months before the restrictions to 17 in the eight months after. Magnet exports to America ran at 512 tonnes in August, down 13 percent on the year, and Chinese customs showed shipments to the US falling another 29 percent in September. General licences introduced last December cover three Chinese producers and exclude any defence end-user. Beijing confirmed on September 28 that the broader truce runs to January 10, 2027, and its statement didn't mention rare earths by name. The suspension that was supposed to lapse on November 10 is, as I write this, formally unextended.

So the chokehold is real. The question is where it sits, and I think most people have the geology wrong. China mines about 60 percent of magnet rare earths. That's a lot, but Mountain Pass in California is one of the richest deposits on earth, Lynas (LYC) mines in Western Australia, and Brazil, Vietnam and Greenland all have ore. Rare earths aren't rare. What China has is 91 percent of separation and 94 percent of sintered magnet production, and separation is the step that matters, because the fifteen lanthanides are chemically near-identical, with the same outer electron configuration and ionic radii that differ by a few picometres down the row. You can't smelt them apart. You pull them apart with thousands of stages of solvent extraction, each stage exploiting a partition coefficient barely above one, and China spent thirty years and a great deal of poisoned groundwater learning to run those cascades at scale. The leverage is a process. Processes are harder to copy than mines and easier to defend than tariffs.

Washington worked this out and did something I didn't expect from this administration: it bought the process. In July 2025 the Pentagon put $400 million into MP Materials (MP) preferred stock and became its largest shareholder, guaranteed a floor of $110 a kilogram for NdPr for ten years, lent $150 million for heavy separation at Mountain Pass, and agreed to buy every magnet from a second Texas plant, 10X, which broke ground in February and should take US capacity to about 10,000 tonnes a year when it's commissioned in 2028. Apple signed for $500 million of recycled magnets from the Fort Worth plant the following week. MP's second quarter showed $17.6 million of price-floor income on NdPr realised in the high nineties, and the first heavy-separation circuit reached mechanical completion in May. If I were going to own this trade I'd own MP and Lynas, which this year is the only producer of separated dysprosium and terbium of any size outside China, at eight tonnes a quarter.

Eight tonnes. The world uses something like 180,000 to 200,000 tonnes of rare earth magnets a year, and the United States imported about 40,000 of them in 2024, more than 90 percent from China. Vacuumschmelze is shipping from South Carolina, Noveon from Texas, and the IEA puts the bill for a diversified supply chain at around $60 billion over a decade, which is less than Meta borrowed in two years. So the money isn't the constraint. The constraint is that a solvent-extraction cascade takes years to commission and a decade to run well, and no fact sheet out of Washington shortens that.
The truce expires on a date in January. The partition coefficients don't expire at all, which is the part I'd keep in mind.

title: The elevator is the only tenant that never leaves
description: Otis sells the elevator at a 5 percent margin and services it at 25 for decades. The annuity hiding inside every building is the actual business.
body: There are about 23 million elevators and escalators in service on earth, and the count grows at a mid-single-digit pace because every new building needs one and almost no old building gives one back. Otis (OTIS) maintains about 2.5 million of them, roughly one in nine. That's the largest service book in the industry, and a smaller share than the company's fame suggests. I've heard "a fifth of the world's elevators" from people who should know better, and I believed it myself until I looked at the filings. It moves 2.5 billion people a day with 72,000 employees, 45,000 of them out in the field with a toolbag.

The share isn't really the number that matters, though. The number that matters is the split between selling an elevator and servicing it. Last year Otis sold $5 billion of new equipment and earned $240 million on it, a margin under 5 percent. It sold $9.4 billion of service, meaning maintenance, repair and modernization, and earned $2.37 billion on that, a record 25.1 percent margin. Service was 65 percent of sales and 91 percent of segment profit. The new elevator is the razor, sold near cost to get into the shaft. The service contract is the blade, sold every month for as long as the building stands, and a building changes owners, tenants and names far more often than it changes its elevator contractor.

In my own field this looks like nucleation and growth. Forming the first droplet of a new phase costs free energy, the barrier is high, and most attempts dissolve. Once a droplet exists above its critical size, growth is downhill and nearly free. Installation is the nucleation event, and Otis pays for it at a 5 percent margin, and everything after that is the cheap downhill part.

The trouble is that nucleation has slowed where it used to happen most. Global new-equipment units fell 6 percent last year to 735,000, driven by a 13 percent drop in China, and Otis's own Chinese new-equipment sales and orders both fell by high-teens percentages last quarter. China is about a fifth of its new-equipment sales and 11 percent of total sales. In July the company cut its 2026 earnings guidance to $4.01 to $4.05 a share from $4.20 to $4.24. The stock is down 18 percent in twelve months to about $75, which is 19 times earnings, with a 2.3 percent dividend, for a $28.6 billion company. Deutsche Bank has it as a short-term sell, Wells Fargo started it at underweight, and the chief executive retires next summer.

I think the sellers have part of this right. A Chinese apartment boom that isn't coming back means fewer razors installed in China for years, and every unit not installed in 2026 is a service contract not signed in 2028 and not renewed in 2040. The damage is real, and it's slow, which is the worst kind for a stock because it never produces the single bad quarter that clears the air.

Where I think they're wrong is that they're pricing a company that earns 91 percent of its profit from service on its 9 percent new-equipment problem. The maintenance portfolio grew 4 percent for the fourth year in a row. Modernization, the business of ripping out a 1990s controller and keeping the shaft, grew 24 percent last quarter with a backlog up 24 percent, because an installed base ages whether or not anyone is building. The 23 million units already installed are the market. The 735,000 new ones a year are closer to marketing.

Otis was spun out of United Technologies on April 3, 2020, three weeks into a pandemic, and has spent six years explaining to a market that wanted a machinery stock that it's a subscription business with a factory attached. I'd rather own the blades than the razor, and at 19 times earnings I'd rather own them a bit cheaper than this, so I'm waiting. But nobody has ever moved into a building and asked who made the elevator. Everybody knows who they call when it stops.

title: The metal that named the trade
description: Up to nine million American homes still drink through lead pipe that was banned in 1986. The rule to remove it runs to 2037, and the pipe is patient.
body: Lead is soft enough to bend around a corner by hand, which is why the Romans ran it under their cities and why the people who did the running were called plumbers: plumbum gave the trade its name. The United States banned new lead water pipe in 1986. By the Environmental Protection Agency's count, up to nine million homes are still connected to the main through the old stuff, and in October 2024 the agency finally wrote the rule that makes water systems dig it out, all of it, within ten years of a compliance date that lands in late 2027. So the last lead service line is scheduled to leave the ground around 2037. A line laid the year before the ban will be fifty-one years old by then.

The chemistry is why this took a century. Lead doesn't leak into water on its own schedule. A pipe carrying properly treated water grows a passivation film on its inner wall, a thin scale of insoluble lead carbonate and phosphate between the metal and your glass, and as long as nobody touches the water chemistry the film holds. Change the source, drop the orthophosphate, let the pH drift, and the film dissolves and the metal comes with it. That's what Flint was, a passivation layer removed. The new rule lowers the action level from 15 to 10 micrograms per litre, but a limit is a measurement, not a fix, and the fix is a trench in front of every house.

The economics aren't close. The agency puts the cost of the rule at $1.5 to $2 billion a year and the benefits at $13 to $25 billion: up to 900,000 infants a year spared low birth weight, 1,500 fewer premature heart deaths, 200,000 IQ points not lost. Thirteen dollars back for one in. No private balance sheet is allowed to make that trade, because the dollar comes out of a water bill in 2029 and the thirteen come back as a child who reads a little better in 2045. So the pipe sat there through the 1991 rule and the 2021 rule and is only now being counted.

What I find strange about water, more than roads or wires, is that it's the one utility where the asset is older than the institution. Roughly 67,000 water systems fall under the rule, most of them small, and the lead under their streets predates the system's charter, its ratepayers, its engineers and often the municipality itself. A power line gets replaced on a depreciation schedule. A lead service line was never on one, because nobody expected to replace it. The plan was to coat it and hope.

Then there's who pays for the trench. Washington put up $15 billion from the 2021 infrastructure law for lead lines specifically and $26 billion usable for lead at all, against an annual bill the agency itself puts near $2 billion for a decade, so the balance lands on the water bill in the towns least able to pay it. The water utilities' own trade association sued over the rule the month it was published, arguing that ten years isn't feasible. The government has defended it through two administrations, briefing closed in April, and the court hears argument this autumn. Meanwhile the rule stands: inventories and first replacements are due November 1, 2027, and the agency issued fresh guidance in August on how to reach the pipes. It sells the programme as 15,500 jobs per billion dollars, which is true and also the wrong reason. The country has about 510,000 plumbers and pipefitters for nine million trenches.

If I wanted to own the shovel rather than the hole, I'd look at Pentair (PNR), which sells the pumps and filters that sit between a dubious main and a kitchen tap, and Advanced Drainage Systems (WMS), which extrudes pipe from recycled plastic for the water that falls on the street rather than the water that comes out of it. Neither has a lead problem. Both get paid when somebody decides to fix one.
The metal named the trade, and so far it has outlasted every rule written about it. I'd like 2037 to be the year that stops being true, and I'm not confident it will be.

title: The panel was never the hard part
description: A module leaves China for under ten cents a watt and then waits years for a wire. The cheap part of solar is the only part that got cheap.
body: In May 2025 China connected 93 gigawatts of solar to its grid in a single month. The modules had fallen below ten cents a watt at the factory gate the year before, a price that buys the tempered glass, the aluminium frame, the encapsulant, the junction box and the sliced silicon that turns photons into current, and the factories were losing money at it. Prices are down more than 60 percent since 2023, margins at the largest producers are around minus ten percent, and the industry has racked up close to $5 billion of cumulative losses since the start of 2024. The cheapest electricity-generating object ever built is being sold below cost by an industry that can't stop.

Every stage upstream is Chinese too: about 92 percent of the world's polysilicon, 98 percent of its wafers, more than 90 percent of its cells, four fifths of its modules, and China is the main maker of the glass and the encapsulant film besides. The IEA expects concentration in the key segments to stay above 90 percent through 2030. First Solar (FSLR) is the one real exception, and it got there by leaving silicon out: a cadmium telluride film a few microns thick deposited straight onto glass in Ohio, which makes it the one large module maker a tariff on Chinese silicon can't touch.

So the panel is solved. Why is solar still hard here? My answer is that the panel is the only part that got cheap, and everything else is priced in American hours and American permits. A rooftop job is a crew, an inverter, racking, an electrician, a permit, a utility inspection and a salesman, and the panel is now a minor line on that invoice. GAF Energy's solar shingles and Tesla's solar roof are both attacks on the labour side of the same problem: if the roofer is already up there, let the roof be the panel. Utility scale is worse. The IEA's own words for the United States are grid queue backlogs and interconnection delays, and a project stuck in a queue pays interest on land it can't energise.

One distinction I wish more people kept straight: a megawatt is a rate and a megawatt-hour is an amount. A 100-megawatt farm makes 100 megawatt-hours in a bright hour and nothing at midnight, and the grid gets paid for the second number while being built for the first.

In a chain of reactions the overall rate is set by the slowest step, and speeding up the fast ones changes nothing. China spent a decade making the panel step effectively instantaneous. The slow step in America is a transformer order, a county permit and a utility engineer with a queue, and Washington has lately made it slower. The residential tax credit died at the end of 2025.
