Utility-scale projects have to be in service by the end of 2027 unless construction began within a year of the new law. Foreign-entity rules now reach into the Chinese supply chain, which is the only supply chain there is, and Chinese cells and modules carry a 50 percent Section 301 tariff on top. The IEA cut its forecast for American solar by almost 40 percent, 140 gigawatts less by 2030, and for residential by almost 70. Constellation (CEG), the country's largest nuclear operator, is the opposite bet and somehow the same bet: firm power from plants that are already connected, where the connection is the asset.

People keep telling me solar quadruples by 2030. It doesn't, at least not in any forecast I can find. The IEA's main case has the world's renewable capacity a little more than doubling, 4,600 gigawatts added between 2025 and 2030 with solar nearly 80 percent of it, and solar's share of the world's electricity going from 8 percent to 15. So call it a doubling, carried by a country with a desert and a grid it orders rather than queues for. China is nearly 60 percent of the growth and will have solar above a fifth of its own generation by 2030.
The sun is free everywhere. The paperwork, it turns out, is priced locally, and that's the number I'd watch.

title: Every path ends in a wire
description: Three mine disasters set up the record copper price. What keeps it there is that every kind of power plant, and every data centre, ends in a wire.
body: On September 8, 2025, about 800,000 tonnes of wet mud moved through the Grasberg Block Cave in Papua and killed seven workers. Freeport-McMoRan (FCX) declared force majeure on the 24th, cut its 2026 guidance for what is the world's second-largest copper mine by roughly 35 percent, and still isn't back at full rates. That was the third big blow of the year. In May a seismic event flooded the Kakula mine in Congo and Ivanhoe (IVN) withdrew its guidance; its 2026 target is now 380,000 to 420,000 tonnes from a complex that was meant to do 550,000. On July 31 a collapse at El Teniente in Chile killed six workers, Codelco suspended the mine's deep expansion in August over seismic risk, and an avalanche there killed two more on October 11. Escondida, the largest copper mine on earth, shut after a fatal accident on September 23.

Benchmark put the Grasberg loss alone at 591,000 tonnes through the end of 2026, about 2.6 percent of a 23-million-tonne world. Global mine output fell 1 percent in the first seven months of the year and Chilean output fell 7 percent. Smelters are so short of concentrate that they're paying miners $272 a tonne to take it, when in a normal year the money flows the other way. Copper started 2026 at $12,423 a tonne, printed $14,875 on September 10, settled at a record $14,822 for cash on October 12, and was sitting near $14,500 in late October, up about a third on a year earlier.

People tell me South America controls this market, and that's true until you count. Chile mined 5.3 million tonnes in 2025 and Peru 2.7 million, 35 percent of the world between them, and Congo at 3.2 million now out-produces Peru. What Chile actually has is a toll booth. Codelco, the state miner, digs about a quarter of the country's copper, booked 26,875 tonnes in 2025 that an internal audit later found it hadn't produced, and mined 11 percent less in the first half of 2026. The royalty law in force since January 2024 takes the effective tax on large miners to about 45 percent. Mining is 57 percent of Chile's exports. A country that dependent on one metal doesn't really control the price. It just hopes the price holds.

The question I started with was what the shortage did to renewables, and the answer is less than I expected, for arithmetic reasons. An electric car carries about 53 kilograms of copper against 22 in a petrol car. At $14.50 a kilogram that's $770 of copper in the EV, and the whole rally of the past year added about $190 to it. Offshore wind uses about eight tonnes per megawatt against roughly one for a coal plant, so a megawatt of turbine carries $116,000 of copper, which is a rounding error on hardware that costs millions per megawatt installed. So the transition didn't get expensive because copper did. Copper got expensive because the transition is real, because a data centre needs 20 to 40 tonnes per megawatt, and because China's grid spending rose 37 percent in the first quarter.

That's the thing neither the climate deck nor the mining deck likes to say out loud. Solar, wind, gas, nuclear and the server hall disagree about everything except the conductor. Whatever makes the electron, copper carries it, with a resistivity only silver beats, and aluminium, the one real substitute, needs about 60 percent more cross-section to do the same job. The energy transition is, to a large degree, a copper trade with a climate label on it, and the label is what gets the subsidy.

One caveat on the record price. More than 700,000 tonnes are sitting in US warehouses, pulled in ahead of a Section 232 tariff decision on refined copper that has been pending since June, and Macquarie expects it to still be pending at New Year. COMEX stocks are up roughly 700 percent since February 2025 and forecasters still pencil in a small surplus for 2026. Some of the all-time high is metal hiding in American sheds.
Three accidents moved the price this year. Whether it stays there depends on the wire more than the mines, and I lean toward the wire.

title: Fourteen centuries of rock
description: Morocco holds 50 of the world's 73 billion tonnes of phosphate, nothing alive can do without it, and the company that digs it has no shares to buy.
body: A conveyor belt about a hundred kilometres long runs from the Bou Craa mine, in the part of Western Sahara that Morocco administers and the International Court of Justice has declined to call Moroccan, down to the Atlantic. It's the longest conveyor in the world, and the dust blowing off it is visible from orbit. Last year 2.02 million tonnes of rock went down that belt onto 36 ships for exactly three buyers, in India, Mexico and New Zealand. Everyone else has dropped away. The European Court of Justice ruled again in 2024 that the Saharawi have to consent, and they haven't.

Bou Craa is only about eight percent of what OCP digs, though. The number that matters is in the Geological Survey's table: of the world's 73 billion tonnes of phosphate rock reserves, Morocco holds 50 billion, about 70 percent. China holds 3.4 billion, the United States one. Under the table, in the flat prose the Survey uses for every commodity, it says there are no substitutes for phosphorus in agriculture. There are none anywhere, as far as I know. The backbone of DNA alternates sugar and phosphate, the molecule every cell spends as energy is a triphosphate, and bone is calcium phosphate. In my own corner of science, the way a cell tells a protein condensate to form or dissolve is to bolt a phosphate group onto the protein. You can pull nitrogen out of the air with enough natural gas, but phosphorus you have to dig out of the ground.

The reserve number misleads in one way, which is that reserves are about the future and production is about the price. China mined 110 million of the world's 250 million tonnes in 2025, Morocco 36, the United States 20. Divide the ground by the digging and China empties its reserve in about thirty years, America in fifty, Morocco in fourteen centuries. And this year's price shock had almost nothing to do with rock anyway. A tonne of diammonium phosphate takes 1.5 to 2 tonnes of rock, 0.4 of sulfur and 0.2 of ammonia, and roughly 44 percent of seaborne sulfur loads in the Gulf. The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively shut for most of the eight months since the American and Israeli strikes of February 28, with transits in the single digits a day against 85 before. Sulfur went from under $100 a ton in 2024 to above $1,000 by late summer. China, which exported 10 million tons of DAP and MAP in 2021, closed its exports in mid-March. Illinois DAP was $929 a ton on October 16, against $600 to $700 through 2024 and the first half of 2025. So Morocco holds the rock, but the sulfur comes from somewhere else, and this year somewhere else was on fire.

Washington was late to notice all this. Since April 2021 the United States had charged a countervailing duty of more than 16 percent on Moroccan phosphate fertilizer, at the petition of Mosaic (MOS), which runs the Florida mines. Texas A&M puts the cost of that to farmers at $6.9 billion over five seasons. On June 29 the president declared an emergency and suspended the duty for eight months, and in August the first Moroccan cargo in five years, 54,000 tonnes of triple superphosphate, docked at New Orleans. The same summer Mosaic curtailed production in Florida and Louisiana for want of sulfur. So the tariff was protecting a producer that can't make the product without the Gulf, against a producer that owns the ground.

The strange part, to me, is the ownership. OCP is 94 percent owned by the Moroccan state, with the rest held by a bank's funds, a pension fund and a university endowment. A 2008 law gives it the sole right to mine phosphate in the kingdom. It took in about $11.4 billion last year, up 17 percent. Its dollar bonds trade in Dublin. Its shares trade nowhere. You can lend to the most consequential monopoly in food, but you can't own it, and I've looked for a way.
The last phosphate mine on earth will be Moroccan. I'd just like there to be a ticker by then.

title: One percent of the light
description: ASML is sold out through 2028 with no competitor and still fell two percent on a half-percent sales miss. I think that's the wrong thing to price.
body: I've been trying to explain to friends why I find ASML more interesting than Nvidia, and it usually goes badly, so let me try it in writing.

Inside an EUV machine a droplet of molten tin about 25 micrometres across falls through a vacuum chamber fifty thousand times a second. A carbon-dioxide laser hits each droplet twice. The first pulse flattens it into a pancake, and the second turns the pancake into a plasma at something like 220,000 degrees Celsius, roughly forty times the surface of the sun. As the tin ions relax they give off light at 13.5 nanometres. That wavelength is the reason the machine exists and also the reason it's so hard to build, because almost everything absorbs it, air and glass included. You can't focus it with a lens. So the machine uses mirrors, about ten of them, each made of around a hundred alternating layers of molybdenum and silicon, and each reflecting at most 68 percent of what hits it. After ten bounces about one percent of the light that left the plasma reaches the wafer. Zeiss spends two to three years polishing each mirror to a roughness measured in picometres, a fraction of an atom. The comparison I've seen is that if you scaled one up to the size of Germany, the tallest bump on it would be under a millimetre.

Exactly one company turns all of that into a machine that works, ASML (ASML), in Veldhoven. A standard EUV scanner costs around $180 million. The High-NA version is about $400 million and only about a dozen exist so far. Intel has put more than a million wafers through its machines, Samsung plans volume production on them in 2028 and TSMC in 2030. Last year ASML recognised revenue on 48 EUV systems and did €32.7 billion of sales. On October 14 it reported a record quarter, €11.7 billion at a 57.5 percent gross margin, €4.1 billion of it EUV. Back in January it had guided 2026 at €34 to €39 billion. It now says €44 to €45 billion, and €44 billion was the bottom of the 2030 range it laid out in November 2024, so it has reached the floor of its own decade plan four years early. The CEO said on the call that supply as planned for 2027 and 2028 won't meet demand, and that customers asking to reserve slots for 2029 and 2030 are being told to wait.

China has never been allowed an EUV machine. The Dutch don't license them, and since 2023 and 2024 the better deep-ultraviolet immersion tools have needed licences too, granted case by case. So Chinese fabs bought the older ones, more than $13 billion worth on roughly 180 NXT:1980i scanners across 2024 and 2025 by one count. China was 41 percent of ASML's system sales in 2024, 33 percent last year and 23 percent in the quarter just reported. There's a bill in Washington, the MATCH Act, introduced in April, that would end even that: all immersion lithography, plus the servicing of tools already installed, with the Netherlands given 150 days to copy the rule or have the foreign direct product rule do it for them. It got folded into the Senate defence bill, and the Senate blocked that bill on July 14 in a fight over paying for the Iran war. So it's stalled, for now.

Here's the part I can't get over. This company, with supply sold out for three years, no competitor to speak of, and customers begging for 2030, fell nearly two percent on October 14 and another two after hours because sales came in at €11.66 billion against a consensus of €11.72 billion. That's a miss of half a percent. The shares have traded between $946 and $2,000 in twelve months, which is the kind of range you'd expect from a semiconductor-equipment cyclical, and to be fair ASML was exactly that for decades, back when fabs ordered scanners in waves and cancelled them in waves. I think the market is still pricing the quarter instead of the queue. At 36 times next year's earnings it isn't cheap, I'll grant that. But its own January guidance turned out to be eight billion euros too low, and the price increases on its most critical tools don't start showing up until 2027.

If I had to own one semiconductor company it would probably be the one that doesn't make semiconductors. I don't own it yet, mostly because I keep waiting for a cheaper entry that the order book says isn't coming.

title: Four hundred to one
description: India trades 394 rupees of derivatives per rupee of stock, nine in ten retail traders lose, and Jane Street made $4 billion there.
body: For every rupee of stock that changed hands on India's exchanges last fiscal year, about 394 rupees of derivatives changed hands on top of it. In 2016 the ratio was 14. The regulator, SEBI, publishes this number itself, in a study it put out in August with the flat title "Profitability of Individual Traders in the Equity Derivatives Segment," which is the bureaucratic way of saying they counted, and the traders lose.

And they do lose. Of the 8.75 million individuals who traded futures and options in the year to March 2026, 87.7 percent finished in the red. Together they lost 91,685 crore rupees, roughly $10 billion, and that was an improvement, because the year before 10.6 million people lost about $13 billion. Over five years the cumulative figure is 3.85 lakh crore, call it $45 billion, transferred from salaried Indians to whoever sat on the other side of the trade. About a third of these traders hold no stock at all. They aren't hedging anything. They're buying weekly Nifty options on their phones more or less the way their fathers bought lottery tickets, except that a lottery pays out in the aggregate and this doesn't.

So who was on the other side? For two years the single most profitable answer was a firm from New York that most of them had never heard of. SEBI's July 2025 order alleged that Jane Street made about 36,500 crore rupees, around $4.3 billion, from Indian index derivatives between January 2023 and March 2025, and that 4,843 crore of that came from manipulating the Bank Nifty index: buy the constituent banks hard in the morning, let the index drag the options with it, hold a much larger short options position, then sell the banks into the close. SEBI barred the firm from the market. Jane Street deposited the $567 million in escrow within two weeks, had the bar lifted within three, and in October was still arguing the merits before the Securities Appellate Tribunal, where it has accused the regulator of moving the goalposts after the fact.

I keep holding those two facts next to each other. The retail base loses on the order of $10 billion a year, and the best trading firm in the world found that market so rich that its 2024 India take, $2.3 billion, was more than a tenth of its global revenue. In 2025 Jane Street booked $39.6 billion in net trading revenue, more than JPMorgan's entire trading operation. India was part of the reason it could.

This is where I part ways with the moralists. SEBI's complaint was never that Jane Street was good at this. It was that one pattern, in one index, crossed the line from aggressive into manipulative, and that's a question for the tribunal. The structural fact is older and stranger. On top of a stock market worth roughly $5 trillion, India has built a derivatives market whose notional turnover runs at four hundred times the underlying, populated by tens of millions of individuals who are statistically certain to lose. There's no other market like it. The United States has a bigger options market in dollars and a far smaller one in participation. Korea had the wildest index options market on earth in 2011 and regulated it into a corner within a year. India's regulator is tightening too, with bigger lot sizes and fewer weekly expiries, and the number of active traders fell 18 percent last year. It's still the largest casino in the world where the house seats are open to anyone with a Mumbai office and a market-making licence.

So I don't think the right lesson for a hedge fund is "stay away." Every quant firm I'd want to own a piece of should have a desk in India and a compliance officer who has read the Jane Street order twice. The edge isn't a trick. The edge is that a country of 1.4 billion people has decided, for now, to pay a toll of about $10 billion a year to whoever is fast enough to collect it, and has posted the tariff in a government PDF. Toll roads are good businesses, and the ones with a published rate are the best ones.

title: A labour-supply request in work boots
description: The people telling teenagers to become electricians are the people who'll be hiring them. A purchase order isn't career advice.
body: In September 2025 the chief executive of Nvidia sat in a British television studio and told the country's teenagers what to do with their lives. "If you're an electrician, you're a plumber, a carpenter, we're going to need hundreds of thousands of them to build all of these factories." The skilled craft segment of every economy, he said, "is going to see a boom." He said it again on Fox Business this August: hundreds of thousands of jobs for "people who build things, that make things with their hands." BlackRock's chief executive told an energy conference in March 2025 that he had warned the White House "we're going to run out of electricians." Blackstone's president promised a "huge boom in blue-collar employment." In July, leaders from BlackRock, Carhartt, Ford and Google formed an Alliance for America's Skilled Trades.

I want to take the pitch seriously first, because the shortage is real. The Census Bureau put data-centre construction at an $85 billion annual rate in August, up 73 percent on the year, while factory construction has fallen 32 percent from its 2024 peak. Electrical work is 45 to 70 percent of a data centre's construction budget, and the electricians' union near Washington has doubled its membership since 2018 to 14,700 and still can't fill its calls. A qualified electrician there earns about $59.50 an hour, better than $120,000 a year with benefits. About 20,000 electricians retire each year. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects electricians to grow 9 percent in the decade to 2035 and plumbers 7 percent, against 3.5 percent for all jobs. None of that is what bothers me.

What bothers me is who's talking and what they're buying. Every voice in that chorus is a buyer of electrical labour or a financier of the buildings that need it. When a customer tells you to increase production, that isn't career guidance. It's a purchase order, written in the language of virtue, real work and hands and things, because a purchase order written in the language of wages would have to name a price and a term. The term is the capex cycle. Four companies will spend about $725 billion on data centres this year. That cycle will end the way capital cycles end, and the message to the eighteen-year-old doesn't come with a date on it.

Then there are the numbers the pitch leaves out. Nine percent growth for electricians is 75,900 jobs over ten years, about 7,600 a year across the whole country. In 2024 the electrical contractors' association counted 120,000 apprenticeship applications, up from 70,000 two years earlier, which is already more than the positions on offer. The pitch has worked. A large data centre employs up to 1,500 people at peak construction and about 50 once it's finished, and one analysis of federal payroll data found as few as 23,000 permanent data-centre jobs nationwide in 2024. The farmers who turn up in the same speeches are the one group projected to shrink, down 3 percent, and ironworkers grow 1 percent. An electrical apprenticeship takes four to five years. In a driven system, a response that takes longer to arrive than the force takes to change is always answering the previous push. In 2008 nearly one in four union construction electricians was out of work. Nobody who gave a speech in 2005 was laid off in 2009.

The equipment side has no such exposure. Caterpillar (CAT) sells the generators behind every server hall, Deere (DE) sells the tractor to a farmer the projections say won't be replaced, and Otis (OTIS) will service the elevators whichever tenant is in the building. Machines get bought once, at the top of the cycle. Labour gets rented while the cycle lasts and handed back when it ends.

So, become an electrician if the work suits you. It's a good trade and I mean that. Just notice that the man on television isn't your guidance counsellor. He's your customer, and he'd like the price to come down.

title: Not on the axis
description: Switch 2 sold 23.7 million units in thirteen months. The stock is down 42 percent, at thirty times a year Nintendo itself says will be worse.
body: On September 1 Nintendo raised the American price of the Switch 2 from $449.99 to $499.99, fifteen months after launch, with the console outselling the PlayStation 5 by more than two to one. Companies don't usually do that in a console's second year. Nintendo (NTDOY) looked at memory prices being driven up by the data-centre build, looked at tariffs, and decided the customer would pay. So far the customer has.

The numbers as of June 30: 23.68 million Switch 2 consoles sold since the June 2025 launch, 19.86 million of them in the first fiscal year against a launch-day forecast of 15 million. Sony's (SONY) PlayStation 5 shipped 1.6 million units in the June quarter. The Switch 2 shipped 3.82 million, and Nintendo described that quarter as down 34 percent, because the launch frenzy it was lapping was so big. The PS5 has 95.3 million consoles in the world after five and a half years, and the Switch 2 is a quarter of the way there after one.

Then the software, which is where the money actually is. Switch 2 owners have bought 58.17 million games, about two and a half per console. The original Switch, at 156.59 million units, ended up carrying ten games each over its life, 1.56 billion in total. Mario Kart World alone has sold 15.39 million copies. The Super Mario Galaxy Movie passed a billion dollars at the box office this spring, and Nintendo's income from licensing its characters more than doubled in the June quarter, to ¥34.8 billion. Sony owns a very good box. Nintendo owns a plumber that three generations recognise on sight.

The index committees file Nintendo under Communication Services, in a sub-industry called Interactive Home Entertainment, next to Netflix and Alphabet rather than next to the companies that make the television it plugs into. I used to think that was a quirk. I now think it's the most accurate thing anyone has said about the company. Nintendo is a media business that happens to manufacture its own distribution.

The way it wins is the way it has won since the Game Boy: it refuses to fight the spec war. Sony and Microsoft compete on one axis, rendering power, and on that axis Nintendo has been losing on purpose since the Wii. The trick is that Nintendo isn't on the axis. It sells a box that's good enough to run Mario, sells the box at a margin rather than as a loss leader, and then sells the software at a much fatter margin for seven or eight years to an installed base no other publisher can reach. Its customers are children. Children become parents, and parents buy the box they remember.

Now the price. The shares closed at ¥14,795 in August 2025 and trade near ¥8,500 today, down about 42 percent, for a market value around ¥9.8 trillion, roughly $63 billion. On trailing earnings that's 21 times. On forward earnings it's about 30, and the gap between those two numbers is the whole argument. Nintendo's own forecast for the year to March 2027 is 16.5 million consoles against 19.86 million, net sales down 11 percent to ¥2.05 trillion, profit down 27 percent to ¥310 billion, with about ¥100 billion of memory and tariff costs written into it. So the market is paying thirty times a year the company itself says will be worse.

Is the market right? Partly, I think. Nintendo guides low as a habit; the 15 million became 19.86 million, and sell-through is running ahead of the original Switch at the same point in its life. But the memory squeeze is real, the price rise will cost some units, and a $500 console is a different purchase from a $450 one in a household already paying more for everything else. I'd own it below ¥8,000, and not as a console cycle. I'd own it as the only media company whose audience gets replaced every seven years and arrives already knowing the characters.
Mario is forty-five years old. His customers are seven, and as far as I can tell they always will be.

title: Three envelopes
description: Three firms own three quarters of chip-design software. Washington put it under licence by letter in May 2025 and handed it back forty days later.
body: On Friday, May 23, 2025, the Bureau of Industry and Security sent Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) a letter. Siemens EDA got one the same day, and the following Thursday Synopsys (SNPS) received its copy and suspended its guidance within hours. A licence was now required to export, re-export or transfer within China any electronic design automation software, including software classed so low on the control list that it normally needed no licence at all. The day the news leaked, Cadence fell 10.7 percent and Synopsys 9.6. Three envelopes, and most of the world's chip design was under licence.

Three was enough because three is basically the whole industry. Synopsys has about 31 percent of global EDA revenue, Cadence about 30, Siemens about 13, which is three quarters of the market and roughly 80 percent of China's. Siemens' Calibre, which checks a layout against a foundry's rules before tape-out, is used by nine in ten chip designers on earth. A chip is a drawing before it's a thing, and the drawing gets made in software owned by two Californian companies and a division of a German conglomerate.

I write Rust for a living, so the way I see this is as the difference between a check at compile time and a check at runtime. Chip controls are runtime checks. A rule names a part number, customs inspects each shipment, and smugglers test the coverage one crate at a time. Controlling the design tools is a compile-time check. Nothing unpermitted gets built, because it never gets drawn. That's what the letters did, and it's why the industry went so quiet. Nobody was told what was still permissible, so the three companies stopped almost everything.

In practice there was a hole, and it's worth being honest about it. Software already installed on a Chinese desk kept running. What stopped was updates, patches and support. The compiler stayed, frozen at its last version, and a frozen compiler designs yesterday's chip forever. That bites hardest at the frontier, where every new node needs new tool releases, and barely at all on the mature nodes where China ships most of its volume. A licence on software is a slow strangulation rather than a cut.

It lasted forty days. On July 2 Synopsys got a second letter saying the restrictions were rescinded, effective immediately. Cadence and Siemens followed a day later. The price was rare earths. Under the framework agreed with Beijing, China would speed up its permits for magnets and critical minerals, and America would let chip-design software, ethane and aircraft engines flow again. So the most complete chokepoint in American technology got spent on a truce over dysprosium. China's hold on rare earths is a chemical process that takes a decade to copy. America's is software, and last summer the two were put on one table and swapped.

The money explains some of it. Synopsys took about $990 million from China in fiscal 2024, 16 percent of its revenue, and Cadence $550 million, 12 percent. Empyrean, the largest Chinese vendor, took about 1.2 billion yuan that year, roughly $170 million, and has sat on the Entity List since December 2024; Primarius and a hundred-odd smaller firms share the rest. Synopsys's China sales alone are nearly six times Empyrean's whole business, and every month under the letters sent Chinese purchase orders to Empyrean instead, which is how a chokepoint ends up funding its own replacement. Synopsys, meanwhile, closed its $35 billion purchase of Ansys in July 2025 and now sells the physics as well as the logic: heat, stress and electromagnetics under the same roof as timing. This year's fight has moved downstream, to lithography tools and who is allowed to service them in China.

If I were going to bet on this, I'd bet on the three rather than on the chips. A chip gets sanctioned by name, one part number at a time. The software it was drawn in has no part number and, at the frontier, no substitute, and the one time Washington picked it up as a weapon, it put it down again after forty days.

title: Four signatures, one hand
description: UnitedHealth is the payer, the doctor, the pharmacist and the rail the money runs on. The fury is a signal. The structure is the actual problem.
body: Sixty-three cents of every dollar Optum Rx booked in 2025 came from another part of UnitedHealth Group (UNH). The pharmacy benefit manager filled 1.66 billion prescriptions and took in $155 billion, and its largest customer is the insurer that owns it. Optum Health employs or affiliates more than 90,000 physicians, about one in ten in the country. Optum Insight owns Change Healthcare, the clearinghouse that moves 15 billion transactions a year and touches one in three patient records. Optum Bank holds the health savings accounts. One company is the payer, the doctor, the pharmacist and the rail the money runs on, and it booked $447.6 billion of revenue in 2025, up 12 percent.

It isn't alone in this. CVS Health owns Aetna and Caremark. Cigna owns Express Scripts. Those three PBMs processed 80 percent of the country's prescription claims last year, and Humana runs the same model at a smaller scale. The industry's word for all this is integration, and the pitch is that one owner holding every step takes the friction out. The way I think about it, a market runs on a difference the way a heat engine does. The insurer and the provider are the hot and cold reservoirs, and the price is the work done between them. Put both in one hand and there's no gradient and no work, only heat, and the heat here is $155 billion of internal billing that nobody outside the building ever negotiated.

The market noticed late. UnitedHealth closed at a record $596 a share in November 2024, worth about $560 billion. In April 2025 it cut its forecast and lost 22 percent in a day. What the release called "heightened care activity" was people using the insurance they had paid for. In May the chief executive left and the guidance went with him. By December the company was worth about $300 billion, and it's back near $370 billion today. The 2025 medical care ratio was 89.1 percent, meaning 89 cents of each premium dollar went to care.

In July 2025 the company disclosed criminal and civil Justice Department investigations into its Medicare billing, widened by August to Optum Rx and to how it pays its own doctors. A Senate Judiciary staff report in January found it captured more diagnosis codes than any other Medicare Advantage insurer and called risk adjustment "a major profit centered strategy." The company disputes that. On denials the record is also the Senate's: UnitedHealthcare's prior-authorization denial rate for post-acute care went from 10.9 percent in 2020 to 22.7 percent in 2022. Across the exchange market, insurers denied 19 percent of in-network claims in 2024, and fewer than one percent of those were appealed.

On December 4, 2024, Brian Thompson, who ran the insurance arm, was shot dead on a Manhattan sidewalk on his way to the company's investor day. That was murder, and nothing in a denial letter or a 10-K excuses it. His killer pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges in August and will be sentenced in December, and the state murder case is stalled on a double-jeopardy motion. What should worry the company more than the trial is the public reaction, which wasn't grief. It told you how many people had met this structure at its worst with nobody to send the anger to, because the insurer, the doctor and the pharmacist were all the same voicemail.

Violence doesn't break a structure like that. If anything it hardens it. A company under threat gets sympathy, a bigger legal budget and a licence to call every critic dangerous. What breaks it is a statute. Arkansas tried in April 2025, banning PBMs from owning pharmacies; a federal judge enjoined the law and the appeal is sitting at the Eighth Circuit. Congress passed PBM transparency in February, effective in 2028, and transparency is what a legislature passes when it has decided not to touch ownership. The FTC settled its insulin case with all three PBMs by June, and no settlement changes who owns whom.
The denial, the diagnosis, the prescription and the cheque all carry a signature, and the four signatures come from one hand. Until that changes, I don't think the rest of it does.

title: Three neutrons, ten years
description: The AI companies are buying power from reactors that already exist. New uranium demand lands in the 2030s, and only the term price has noticed.
body: Earlier this month, in Covert Township, Michigan, workers lowered fuel assemblies back into a reactor that was shut in 2022 and sold to be dismantled. The Energy Secretary toured Palisades and said it will be running within weeks, on up to $1.52 billion of federal loan guarantees. In Pennsylvania, Constellation (CEG) expects fuel on site by year-end for the 835-megawatt unit it has renamed Crane and everyone else still calls Three Mile Island, under a twenty-year contract to sell the output to Microsoft. No shuttered American reactor has ever come back before. Two are coming back now, one of them for a software company.

If you count the gigawatts the AI companies have signed for and then count the ones that are actually new, the gap is most of the story. Meta's 6.6 gigawatts by 2035, announced in January, is more than 2.1 from Vistra (VST) plants that have run for decades, 1.2 from an Oklo campus pencilled in for 2030 at the earliest, and TerraPower reactors due no sooner than 2032. Amazon's 1,920 megawatts from Talen's (TLN) Susquehanna comes out of a plant already on the grid. Every deal has the same shape, output from reactors that already hold fuel, and a change of customer isn't a change of demand.

That's what explains the strangest chart in commodities right now. The long-term contract price, the one utilities actually pay, ended September at $96.50 a pound, a nominal record above the $95 of 2007. Spot sat near $90. Uranium equities are down over 20 percent in a year, and the Sprott trust that does nothing but hold the metal traded this month at an 11.6 percent discount to what it holds. The term price is being set by people buying fuel for 2030. The equities are being set by people who wanted the trade to pay in 2026 and have given up. I side with the fuel buyers, for whatever that's worth.

Supply sits mostly in one place. Kazakhstan produced 25,839 tonnes of uranium in 2025, about 40 percent of the world, nearly all of it by pumping sulphuric acid into sandstone, 70 to 80 kilograms of acid per kilogram of metal. Kazatomprom (KAP) has cut its nominal 2026 capacity by about 10 percent, and Rosatom's Uranium One owns half or more of several of its mines. Mines covered about 90 percent of reactor requirements in 2024, and the rest came out of stockpiles, which don't refill.

But I don't think the mine is the chokepoint. The chokepoint is three neutrons. Natural uranium is about 0.7 percent U-235, a reactor wants 3 to 5, and the only route from one to the other is to turn the metal into uranium hexafluoride gas and spin it. Fluorine has a single stable isotope, so the whole difference between a molecule carrying U-235 and one carrying U-238 is three neutrons in roughly 350 mass units, and a centrifuge exploits that a sliver at a time, in cascades thousands of machines long.

Rosatom owns about 29 million of the world's 68 million separative work units, 43 percent. American utilities bought 26 percent of their enrichment from Russia in 2025, under a 2024 law that bans the trade and whose waivers expire on January 1, 2028. Urenco adds 700,000 units in New Mexico by early 2027. Centrus (LEU), with a $900 million federal contract signed in July, expects no new commercial capacity before 2029.

Here are the dates laid out in a row, which is how I finally understood it. Power contracts signed in 2024 through 2026. Restarts fuelled in 2026 and 2027. Russian waivers lapse at the start of 2028. Western centrifuge halls arrive from 2029. The first reactors that are new rather than renamed arrive between 2030 and 2035, and a thousand-megawatt unit then wants about 140,000 separative work units a year for the rest of its life. None of that is priced into a share of Cameco (CCJ) trading on this quarter's spot. If I were putting money on it, it'd be Cameco and Centrus, held through the stretch where nothing appears to happen, which is the hard part.
The fuel going into Palisades this month already exists. The fuel that matters doesn't yet, and neither do the centrifuges that will spin it.

title: The doll was a surveillance device
description: Germany banned a talking doll under its spy-equipment law. Alexa took the kitchen with almost no intelligence. Owning the room beats being smart.
body: In February 2017 the German Federal Network Agency, which regulates telecoms, ordered a blonde doll called My Friend Cayla off the shelves, on the grounds that an object which conceals a microphone and transmits what it hears is a prohibited surveillance device. Genesis Toys sold the doll, Nuance handled the speech, and the Bluetooth link had no authentication, so anyone within range could pair with a child's toy and listen. The regulator wasn't making a metaphor. It applied the law written for hidden bugs to a product in the toy aisle, and the law fit.

A year later the Federal Trade Commission settled with VTech for $650,000 over a tablet system that collected the names, birthdates and genders of hundreds of thousands of children without parental consent, had been breached in 2015, and had told parents the data was encrypted when none of it was. Last September the FTC charged Apitor, a Shenzhen maker of robot toys, with letting a Chinese analytics kit called JPush pull precise location from thousands of children through its app; the $500,000 penalty was suspended because the company said it couldn't pay. Then came the chatbot plush. The Kumma bear from FoloToy, sold as running on GPT-4o, told testers how to find and light matches before moving on to sexual topics. OpenAI cut the developer off in November, and by February the bear was still on sale offering GPT-5.1. Mattel announced its OpenAI partnership in June 2025, said its first product would arrive by year-end, then said not that holiday season after all. These toys are sensors pointed at the youngest people in the house, and the business model requires them to be.

Which brings me to the sensor that actually won. Amazon put the Echo on sale on November 6, 2014, at $199, or $99 for Prime members with an invitation. It had seven microphones and almost no mind: music, weather, alarms, pitched fairly honestly as a whole-home Siri. The Wall Street Journal later put the devices division's losses from 2017 through 2021 above $25 billion. Amazon could sell the hardware at a loss because the product was really a microphone in the kitchen with a Prime account attached, and it has since shipped more than 600 million Alexa devices. Now imagine the opposite: a device arriving in 2025 with a frontier model inside, much smarter. I think it would have lost. The intelligence was always something you could add later, and the countertop wasn't. Alexa+ reached everyone in the United States on February 4 this year, free with Prime, and 97 percent of the devices Amazon ever shipped can run it. A dumb device that owns the room gets upgraded into a smart one. A smart device that shows up late has to go and find a room.

The way I'd describe it is as a phase transition. A room with a listening device in it is a different state of matter from a room without one, and the energy barrier is the first installation. Once the microphone is there, making it cleverer costs a software push. Making a cleverer microphone appear in that same kitchen costs a second purchase that nobody makes.

That's why I don't think the ethics of the toy aisle are a side issue. Mattel and its imitators aren't competing on intelligence, since the intelligence is rented from the same handful of labs. They're competing to be the first microphone a child trusts, and the retention policies tell you what the prize is. The amended children's privacy rule took full effect on April 22. A bill to update the underlying law passed the Senate unanimously in March and is stalled in the House. The German regulator understood in 2017 what the American market still prices as a feature: a device that hears a child is a device that hears a child, whatever face it's wearing.
Cayla has been illegal in Germany for nine years. The room she was built to occupy got taken by a speaker, and I'm not sure anyone noticed.

title: Bug me last
description: The order an agent should look things up in: memory, an API, search, the browser, and then me. I'm the most expensive step and the least reliable.
body: Every time an agent stops to ask me something it could have figured out on its own, I learn something about how it was built. The question is almost never hard. Which directory is the config in. JSON or YAML. Should I go ahead. What the question gives away is a lookup order, and the lookup order is wrong.

The order I actually want is this. Check memory first, meaning whatever has already been established in this project, this session, this repo. After that, the APIs: structured, typed, authenticated endpoints that give back an exact answer in milliseconds. Search comes next, wide but noisy. The browser is after that, slow and visual and only worth it for pages that refuse to be anything but pages. And then, only then, me.

I think of it as a cost gradient. Memory is free. An API call costs a round trip and gives you a fact with a schema attached. Search costs a round trip too but gives you ten guesses. A browser session costs seconds per click and gives you pixels. And a human costs minutes of latency at best, hours if I'm asleep, and what comes back is itself a guess, because by that point I usually know less about the state of the task than the agent does. I'm the most expensive oracle in the stack and the least reliable one, and I'd like to be treated that way.

The industry has this backwards, and I think it's because of a confusion about what politeness is. Products that interrupt constantly get described as keeping the human in the loop. That sounds like respect. In practice it works as a way of passing the blame along. If the agent asks before every step, nothing it does is ever its fault. I don't think that's safety. It's a design that has handed its judgment to the person least able to exercise it, at the moment they're least able to, and then called the result alignment.

There's a narrower version of the loop that I'd actually sign up for. Ask me when the action can't be undone and the choice is a real fork: deleting something, sending something, spending money, publishing. The other case is when the task as stated contradicts itself and no amount of reading will resolve it. Otherwise, climb the ladder. Check what you already know. Hit the endpoint. Search. Open the page if you really have to. Take the most reasonable reading, write down at the top of your work which reading you took so I can see it, and keep going.

I've been building a command framework in Rust where this is enforced by the compiler rather than by a prompt. The system definition gets generated from the plugin's own types at build time, so a bound that won't typecheck is a compile error instead of a surprise at registration. The idea is the same as the ladder: push every question as far upstream as it will go. If memory has the answer, resolve it there. If the type system can catch it, let the compiler do it. Failing that, put it in a schema. Whatever's left over goes to the human, and the measure of the system, as far as I'm concerned, is how little is left over.

An agent that bugs me last hasn't stopped being careful. It has spent its care on the rungs where care is cheap, so that by the time it gets to me it's carrying a decision rather than a question. That's the version I want to build, and the one I want to use.

title: The sticker does the work
description: A television doesn't change when it goes back through the return door. Its price does. A lot of investing is just noticing that gap.
body: I bought a 65-inch television in June, kept it for eleven days, and took it back. There was nothing wrong with it. The pixels didn't age in my living room. But once something comes back through the return door the store can't sell it as new anymore, so a second sticker goes on the box that says open box, and open box means a discount, and the discount is often large.

So here's a small game I play. Buy the television. Return it inside the window, intact, receipt in hand. Go back a few days later and find the same unit on the clearance rack wearing the second sticker. Buy it again. I pay cash on at least one leg, preferably both, partly because I'd rather the loyalty database not draw a line between the two transactions, and partly because a game the store would rather you didn't play is still a game you're allowed to play.

I'm not writing this up to teach anyone how to save a few hundred dollars on a Hisense. I'm writing it because it's the cleanest demonstration I know of something most people never quite absorb, which is that price isn't a property of the object. Price is a story the seller tells about the object, and the story can get rewritten by events that never touch the thing itself.

Physicists have a name for a quantity that depends only on the state of a system and not on its history: a state function. The television is one of those. Its price isn't, because the price carries a path with it: who held it, for how long, whether a box got opened, whether a form got filled in. The retailer's accounting can't see the panel, only the path.

Markets do the same thing at scale, every day, with better instruments. A bond gets cut one notch below investment grade and every fund whose mandate forbids junk has to sell it that week, whether or not a single cash flow changed. When a stock drops out of an index, the index funds dump it on rebalance day. One bad quarter and the word distressed goes on the box. The cash flows are the same and the sticker is new, and someone who's only permitted to own clean boxes has to sell to someone who's willing to look inside.

That second buyer is who I try to be. Not because open boxes are always bargains. They aren't, and sometimes the panel really is cracked. But the discount for a damaged label is paid by people who aren't allowed to check and collected by people who are, and I'd rather be in the second group.

The return desk, I've decided, is the most honest counter in the store. It's the one place where the seller admits in writing that the first price was only ever a story. The TV, for what it's worth, works fine.
